title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: # The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Most failed migrations I have seen did not fail during the migration. They failed about five weeks later, when someone asked a question nobody could answer: *who gave that subscription permission to create a public load balancer?*

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The answer is almost always that the landing zone was built in parallel with the first wave, by the same two people, under deadline. It worked well enough to get workload one across. It did not survive workload forty.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: So this is the checklist. Eleven things that have to be true before the first production workload moves. None of them are exotic. The reason to write them down is that under migration pressure, four or five always get deferred, and the deferred ones are the ones that produce the five-week-later question.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 1. Identity exists before compute exists

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: If your first VM lands before your identity model does, every later access decision is a retrofit.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Concretely, before anything moves:

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text:
- Workload identities are federated to your existing IdP. No standalone cloud
  accounts with local credentials, not even for the pilot.
- Human access is role-assumption only, time-bounded, with no standing
  privileged access.
- Every role has a named owner. Not a team — a person.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The test: can you answer "which humans could have modified this resource yesterday?" with a query rather than an investigation? If not, stop.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 2. The account/subscription boundary is a blast radius decision

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: People choose account topology for billing clarity, then discover they chose their blast radius too.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The rule we use: **one account per workload per environment**, not one account per team. Teams reorganise; workloads have lifecycles. A workload-scoped boundary means decommissioning is `delete account`, which is the only decommissioning that ever actually happens.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Tags are for reporting. Accounts are for control. Do not try to use tags for control; they are editable by the people you are controlling.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 3. Guardrails are preventive, not detective

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: A detective control tells you someone created an unencrypted bucket. A preventive control means they could not.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Both have a place, but the first wave needs preventive, because during a migration your detective alerts go to a queue nobody is reading. Minimum set, enforced at the organisation level so a workload account cannot opt out:

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text:
- No public object storage, by policy, with an explicit exception process that
  requires a second approver.
- Encryption at rest mandatory, with keys in your KMS, not the provider default.
- Region allowlist. This catches more mistakes than you would expect, and it is
  also your data-residency control.
- No IAM user creation. Federation only, as per item 1.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 4. Network is designed for the steady state, not the migration

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: This is the one that bites hardest. Migration-period networking is temporary: a big fat link back to the data centre, permissive routing, flat address space, because you need everything to reach everything while it is half-moved.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Then the migration ends and that topology is production. Nobody unwinds it, because unwinding it is a project with no feature in it.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Design the steady state first, then design the migration overlay as an explicitly temporary thing with a removal ticket attached:

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text:
```
# Steady state: hub-spoke, spokes cannot route to each other
# Migration overlay: spoke -> on-prem via hub, TAGGED FOR REMOVAL
#
# The overlay routes carry an expiry tag. A weekly job opens a ticket
# for every overlay route older than its expiry. Crude, but it is the
# only thing that has ever actually got them removed.
```

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Address space: allocate assuming three times the workloads you are migrating. You will re-use this account structure for things that were never in the data centre, and renumbering later is a genuine outage.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 5. Cost attribution works on day one, not day ninety

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: If the first invoice arrives and you cannot split it by workload, you have lost the ability to have a cost conversation for the rest of the programme. Finance will ask "why is cloud expensive" and the only available answer will be a shrug.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Mandatory tags, enforced preventively (you cannot create the resource without them): `workload`, `env`, `owner`, `cost-centre`. Enforced, not requested — a tagging policy without enforcement produces a tag coverage of about 60%, which is the same as zero for attribution purposes.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: This matters more than it sounds. Almost every "cloud is more expensive than we thought" conversation is really an attribution failure, which is why [cloud cost is an architecture problem](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem) rather than a procurement one — you cannot fix a structure you cannot see.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 6. Logging goes somewhere the workload account cannot delete

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Audit logs in the account being audited is not an audit trail. Central logging account, write-only from workload accounts, separate retention policy, different access path.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The specific failure this prevents: an incident where you need to know what happened, in an account where what happened included someone with broad permissions.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 7. There is a defined path to production, and it is the only one

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Before the first wave, the deployment path exists and is used by the pilot workload: source control → CI → artefact → environment promotion. No console deploys to production. No exceptions for the migration.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The migration will generate enormous pressure to make exceptions, because console-deploying one thing takes ten minutes and wiring it through the pipeline takes two days. The two days are the point. Everything that goes in through the console stays undocumented forever.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Short-lived credentials for the pipeline, federated via OIDC rather than stored keys — I wrote up the mechanics of that separately, since it is the single highest-value control you can add to a CI system.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 8. Backup and restore are tested, in that order

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Everyone configures backup. The checklist item is **restore**, performed once, on the pilot workload, with the time recorded.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The recorded time is what you give the business when they ask about RTO. Not the number from the provider documentation — your number, from your attempt, with your data volume and your dependencies.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 9. Observability exists before the thing you need to observe

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Migrating a workload into an environment with no dashboards means your first production incident is also your first attempt at instrumentation.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Baseline before wave one: infrastructure metrics, application logs with a correlation ID that survives the service boundary, and one synthetic check per workload that exercises a real user path. Not a health endpoint that returns 200 — a path that touches the database.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 10. Somebody owns the landing zone as a product

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Not a project. A product, with a backlog, a version, and a person whose job includes it after the migration ends.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The alternative — landing zone as a project deliverable — produces an environment that is correct on the day the project closes and drifts from that day onward, with no mechanism to pull it back.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## 11. The first wave is deliberately boring

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The pilot workload should be the one with the least business risk and the most representative architecture. Those two usually conflict, and people resolve the conflict by picking something trivially simple — a static site, an internal tool with four users.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: That teaches you nothing. A static site does not exercise identity, data migration, cross-account networking or the restore path. Pick something dull but *structurally complete*: a service with a database, an external dependency and a scheduled job. Boring in business terms, complete in architectural terms.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: ## Running the checklist

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: We treat these as gates, not suggestions. The first wave does not start with items outstanding, and the way that holds up under deadline pressure is that the gate is reviewed by someone who is not responsible for the deadline.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Items 1-6 are the ones that are expensive to retrofit. 7-11 are expensive to skip. If you only have time for six, take 1-6 and accept that you will be fixing 7-11 during the migration rather than before it.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: Microsoft's [Cloud Adoption Framework landing zone guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/) covers the same ground in more depth and with Azure specifics; it is worth reading even if you are on AWS, because the reasoning is portable and the enforcement primitives map closely.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: For how this fits into the wider sequence — assessment, wave planning, the 7 Rs decision per application, and what to modernise during the move versus after — Pixorama published [the full step-by-step migration strategy](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud), which is where this checklist sits as step two.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: If you are running this with outside help rather than in-house, the thing to test a partner on is whether they treat the landing zone as a product with an owner or as a project deliverable. Their [survey of DevOps consulting firms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india) is a reasonable place to start a shortlist, and that question separates the candidates faster than anything on their websites.

title: The landing zone checklist we run before any migration wave
text: The thing I would most want to convince you of: the landing zone is not preparation for the migration. It is the migration's only durable output. The workloads were going to end up in the cloud either way. Whether they end up somewhere governable is decided entirely in the weeks before the first one moves.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: # The cloud migration that cost more after we finished

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: We finished a migration on time. Ninety-one workloads out of two data centres, fourteen months, every wave inside its window. The programme closed, people were thanked, and somebody made a slide with a green tick on it.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Four months later the monthly infrastructure bill was 18% higher than the data-centre run rate it replaced.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Nobody had lied in the business case. The compute forecast was almost exactly right — within 6%, which for a fourteen-month projection is good. The storage forecast was fine. What we had done was model the cloud as a cheaper place to run the same thing, which is the one assumption that guarantees this outcome.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: I want to be specific about where the money went, because the generic version of this story — "cloud cost optimisation is important" — is useless. The actual causes were four, they were all architectural, and three of them were decided before the first workload moved.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## 1. We paid for a hybrid period we told ourselves was temporary

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The wave plan moved applications in order of business risk. Low-risk first, critical last. Sensible, and it is what every methodology recommends.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: It also meant that for eleven of the fourteen months, roughly a third of our application dependencies ran across the boundary between the cloud and a data centre. Every one of those calls was a charge. Reads that had been free on our own switched network became metered egress.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The number was about $11,000 a month, averaged over the hybrid period. We had budgeted zero, because at planning time nobody asked what the traffic between wave 2 and wave 9 looked like.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The information was available. Flow logs existed. We had a dependency inventory. What we did not have was anyone joining those two things and multiplying by a price, which is an afternoon's work and would have changed the wave order.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The fix is not better forecasting. It is sequencing applications by *data adjacency* rather than business risk, which is a different plan with a different order and some uncomfortable conversations about moving a critical workload in wave 3.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## 2. Lift and shift preserved the shape of a sizing decision made in 2017

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: About sixty of the ninety-one workloads were rehosted essentially as-is. That was deliberate — a time-bound exit from a lease, and rehosting is the fastest way out.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: What it meant in practice: those VMs were sized for hardware bought in 2017 on a three-year refresh cycle, which means they were sized for peak load plus a growth margin plus a safety margin, because adding capacity meant a purchase order and a six-week lead time.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: That sizing logic is completely rational on owned hardware. The cost of over-provisioning is a one-off capital inefficiency, and the cost of under-provisioning is an outage you cannot fix quickly. Of course you oversize.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: In the cloud that same logic is a recurring monthly charge for capacity you do not use, and the under-provisioning risk it was protecting against no longer exists, because you can resize in minutes.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: We rehosted the machines *and the assumption*. Average CPU utilisation across that estate, measured six months in, was 11%.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The honest version of the lift-and-shift decision is: this is a migration strategy, not a cost strategy, and it defers the cost work rather than avoiding it. We knew that. We said it in the steering committee. What we did not do was put a date and an owner on the deferred work, so it did not happen.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## 3. Nobody could tell which team's spend was which

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The first invoice was one number. By the third month people were asking why cloud was expensive, and the only available answer was a breakdown by service type — so much compute, so much storage, so much data transfer.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: That is not an answer anyone can act on. "Compute is 40% of the bill" does not tell a team that their batch job runs on an instance three sizes too large.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Tagging had been part of the landing zone design. It was a *policy* rather than an *enforcement* — resources were supposed to carry owner and cost-centre tags. Actual coverage, when we finally measured it, was 58%.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Fifty-eight percent coverage is functionally zero for attribution, because the 42% is not randomly distributed. It is concentrated in things created in a hurry during cutover weekends, which is also where the oversized instances are.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: We spent six weeks retro-tagging. Some resources we could not attribute at all and had to trace through CloudTrail to find who created them. Two we switched off to see who complained.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Making tags mandatory at creation — the resource simply cannot exist without them — is a one-line policy change that would have saved all of it. It feels bureaucratic in month one. It is the difference between having a cost conversation and having an argument.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## 4. The architecture had a cost shape, and we had never looked at it

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: This is the one that actually mattered, and it is why the other three kept coming back.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Six months post-migration we ran a cost-optimisation programme. Rightsizing, reserved capacity, deleting orphaned volumes, scheduling non-production environments off overnight. It worked: the bill came down 23% in a quarter.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Then it went back up over the following two quarters, to roughly where it had been.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Because none of that touched the structure. The things we fixed were consequences. The causes were a multi-AZ messaging cluster replicating across zones on every write, a reporting service pulling full table extracts from another service's database because there was no event stream, a batch pipeline re-reading the same reference data forty times per run, and a chatty service boundary in a request path that had been drawn around team ownership rather than data locality.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Every one of those is a recurring cost generated by a design decision. Pricing levers reduce the unit cost of running them. They do not stop you running them.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: This is the part I would most want to transplant into the head of anyone about to start: the cloud bill is a readout of your architecture. It is [a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem) over a design problem, and a cost programme that only pulls pricing levers buys exactly one good quarter.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## What we would do differently

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: Not "plan better". Four specific things, in the order they would happen:

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: **Join the flow logs to the wave plan, before the wave plan is approved.** Price every cross-boundary dependency by the number of months it will span the boundary. Resequence around the top five. This is an afternoon and it was worth about $120,000 on this programme.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: **Make the lift-and-shift deferral explicit, with a date.** "Rehost now, rightsize within 90 days of each wave, owner named per workload." The deferral is fine. The deferral without a date is how 11% utilisation survives for a year.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: **Enforce tags preventively, not by policy.** Cannot create the resource without `workload`, `env`, `owner`, `cost-centre`. Accept the friction in week one.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: **Cost-review the architecture, not the invoice.** Once per quarter, pick the three largest line items and ask what design decision produces them. Not "can we get a discount on this" — "why does this exist". The answers are usually a missing cache, a missing event stream, or a service boundary in the wrong place.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: ## The part that is genuinely hard

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: I do not want to make this sound like a process failure with a process fix.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The real difficulty is that the people who can see the cost shape of an architecture are the architects, and they are fully occupied with the migration; while the people who own the cost conversation are in finance, and they cannot read an architecture. The gap between those two groups is where this money goes, and no amount of dashboards closes it — dashboards give finance more detailed numbers about things they still cannot act on.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: What closed it for us, eventually, was putting one engineer in the monthly finance review with a standing agenda item: here are the three largest cost drivers, here is the design decision behind each, here is what changing it would cost in engineering time. That meeting is where the batch pipeline got its cache and the reporting service got its event stream.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: It took us two years to set that meeting up. It should have existed in month one, before the migration started, so that the hybrid-period egress forecast had somewhere to be discussed.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: If you are at the planning stage of one of these, [we wrote the whole process up properly](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) — the assessment work, how to choose a strategy per application rather than per programme, how to sequence waves, and what to modernise during the move versus after. The part I would read twice is the assessment phase, because almost everything in this post was knowable there and we did not look.

title: The cloud migration that cost more after we finished
text: The migration itself was a success, for what it is worth. Ninety-one workloads, on time, no major incident. We just measured it against the wrong thing.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: # Issue 1: What we mean by "the software backbone"

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: This is a fortnightly letter about what engineering decisions cost. Not what they cost in the business case — what they cost when the invoice arrives, or when the migration is finished and the bill went up, or when the rewrite reaches month fourteen.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: I work at a firm that builds and modernises systems for mid-size and large companies. That means I spend most of my time in the gap between what a plan said and what happened, which turns out to be the most interesting place to stand.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Over ten issues I want to make one argument from ten directions. Here it is, and then I will tell you what I am not going to do.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: ## The claim

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: **Almost every expensive technology surprise is a structural decision showing up late.**

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Not a mistake. Not incompetence. A decision that was reasonable when it was made, whose cost arrives in a different quarter, in a different currency, to a different department — by which time nobody connects the two.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Three examples, each of which I will take properly in a later issue:

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: A company migrates to the cloud. Compute is forecast accurately. The bill goes up, because for eleven months a third of their dependencies ran across the boundary between two data centres and nobody priced the traffic. The structural decision was the wave order, made at planning time by business risk. The cost arrived as a line item called "data transfer" eight months later.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: A team adds people to a legacy system to go faster. For two months output falls, because the senior engineers who could have shipped are answering questions instead. The structural decision was treating "backend engineer" as a fungible unit. The cost arrived as a missed quarter.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: A company fine-tunes a model so it will stop getting the return policy wrong. It gets the policy wrong more confidently. The structural decision was confusing knowledge with behaviour. The cost arrived as a customer complaint about an answer that was stated very firmly.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: In every case the information needed to avoid it was available at the time, and in every case nobody was looking at it, because the question had been assigned to a different function.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: ## Why "backbone"

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: The firm I work for uses the phrase "the software backbone of ambitious enterprises", which is marketing language, and I want to rescue what is true in it.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: What is true: in most companies past a certain size, there is a set of systems that everything else depends on, and almost nobody is responsible for their shape. There are people responsible for features. People responsible for uptime. People responsible for cost. Nobody responsible for whether the thing is *coherent*.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: So the shape drifts. Each individual decision is locally sensible. The sum is a system where a reporting query locks tables during business hours, where two services disagree about whether a discount applies to shipping, where the only person who understands the billing logic is six months from retirement.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: That incoherence is what eventually gets called "legacy", and by then the conversation is about replacing it, which is usually the wrong conversation.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: ## What I am not going to do

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: **No predictions.** I do not know what AI will do to software engineering and neither does anyone writing confidently about it.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: **No tool reviews.** Which vector database, which framework, which cloud. These decisions matter much less than the ones around them, and writing about them is how a newsletter becomes an affiliate business.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: **No case studies with the names changed and the numbers improved.** When I give a figure, I will say where it came from and how many instances it is drawn from. When it is three projects, I will say three projects. The ratios transfer; the absolute numbers often do not.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: **No selling.** I work for a company that does this for money, and I am not going to pretend otherwise — the disclosure is at the bottom of every issue. But this is not a funnel. If I have written something that only makes sense as a lead magnet, I have failed at the brief I set myself, and you should tell me.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: ## What I would like from you

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Disagreement, mostly. The claim above is falsifiable: if you have an expensive technology surprise that was *not* a structural decision arriving late, I want to hear it, because that is the most useful thing anyone could send me.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: I will also take requests. If there is a decision you are facing that fits the shape of this — a thing that looks cheap now and you suspect is not — reply and I will think about it in public.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: ## The ten issues

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Roughly, and I reserve the right to change my mind:

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text:
1. This one.
2. The four numbers that decide a migration.
3. Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first.
4. The modernisation decision tree I actually use.
5. Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they do not.
6. Retrieval is a product problem.
7. How to buy engineering capacity.
8. Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team.
9. Security that does not stop delivery.
10. How to run a vendor shortlist.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Two and three are the ones I have the most data on. Five is the one where I am most likely to be wrong, and I will say so when I get there.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: Next issue in a fortnight.

title: Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
Issue 1: What we mean by 'the software backbone'
text: *I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/), where I work on cloud and platform engineering. Everything here is my own view and my own reading of the projects I have been on. Where I use numbers from client work they are anonymised and rounded, and I will tell you how many instances they come from.*

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: # Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Every migration programme produces a wave plan in a spreadsheet. Wave 1, wave 2, wave 3, with applications assigned to each and a date on top. And every migration programme discovers somewhere around wave 3 that an application in wave 5 is a synchronous dependency of an application in wave 2, so either wave 2 is not done or wave 5 just moved.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: This is not a diligence failure. It is a representation failure. Dependencies form a directed graph, and a spreadsheet cannot hold a graph — it can only hold one flattening of it, chosen before you knew which flattening was feasible.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: So: build the graph, compute the waves, regenerate when the graph changes.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: ## What you need from the CMDB

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Less than you think. Three things:

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text:
```
applications:  id, name, criticality, owner, data_classification
dependencies:  source_app, target_app, kind (sync | async | batch | data)
constraints:   app_id, kind (freeze_window | licence | compliance | hardware_eol), detail
```

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Your CMDB is wrong, by the way. Everyone's is. Expect 20-40% of dependencies to be missing. The graph is still worth building, because a graph with known gaps beats a spreadsheet with unknown ones — and the graph tells you *where* to spend your discovery budget, which is the part that actually reduces risk.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Supplement from flow logs, which do not lie about what talks to what:

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text:
```python
# Netflow/VPC-flow-derived edges, intersected with CMDB-declared edges.
# The interesting set is the difference, not the union.
declared = set(cmdb_edges)
observed  = set(flow_edges)

undeclared = observed - declared   # these are your real risk
stale       = declared - observed  # these may be decommissioned, verify
```

text: ## Dependency kinds are not equal

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: The single most useful modelling decision: edge weight by coupling type, because they constrain the plan differently.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text:
- **`sync`** — A calls B and waits. If they are separated across the WAN, A's
  latency budget absorbs the round trip. These must move together or you must
  accept the latency. Hard constraint.
- **`async`** — A queues to B. Tolerates separation well, as long as the queue
  is reachable from both sides. Soft constraint.
- **`batch`** — A reads B's extract nightly. Tolerates separation for a whole
  day. Nearly free.
- **`data`** — A and B share a database. These are not two applications for
  migration purposes; they are one unit. Collapse them.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Collapse `data` edges first. It usually shrinks the node count by 15-25% and removes most of the apparent cycles.

```python
def report_cycles(g):
    sccs = [c for c in nx.strongly_connected_components(g) if len(c) > 1]
    for c in sorted(sccs, key=len, reverse=True):
        print(f"cycle of {len(c)}: {sorted(c)}")
    return sccs
```

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: The first time you run this on a real estate, you will find one SCC with somewhere between 8 and 40 members. That is your monolith, and it does not matter that the architecture diagram shows it as separate applications.

text: This output is the single most valuable artefact of the whole exercise, because it reframes the question. You are no longer asking "which wave does app X go in?" You are asking "do we move these 23 things in one weekend, or do we spend six weeks breaking three edges first?"

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: That is a [legacy application modernization](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization) question rather than a migration question, and it is much better to meet it in planning than in wave 3.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: ## Computing waves

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: With cycles collapsed, the graph is a DAG, and waves are a topological generation walk — but inverted. Dependencies move *first*, so you want to layer from the leaves of the dependency direction:

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text:
```python
def compute_waves(g, max_wave_size=12):
    """Wave N contains apps whose sync/data dependencies are all in waves < N."""
    hard = nx.DiGraph()
    hard.add_nodes_from(g.nodes)
    hard.add_edges_from(
        (u, v) for u, v, k in g.edges(data="kind") if k in ("sync", "data")
    )

    waves, placed = [], set()
    while len(placed) < hard.number_of_nodes():
        ready = [
            n for n in hard.nodes
            if n not in placed
            and all(dep in placed for dep in hard.successors(n))
        ]
        if not ready:
            raise ValueError("cycle remains — collapse SCCs first")

        # Deterministic, risk-ascending order within the wave
        ready.sort(key=lambda n: (
            g.nodes[n].get("criticality", 99),
            -hard.out_degree(n),
            n,
        ))
        wave = ready[:max_wave_size]
        waves.append(wave)
        placed.update(wave)
    return waves
```

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Two details that matter more than the algorithm:

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: **`max_wave_size`** is a capacity constraint, not an architectural one. Set it from how many applications your migration team can actually cut over in a window. Twelve is a reasonable starting guess for a team of six with a weekend window; measure after wave 1 and correct.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: **Sorting by ascending criticality within a wave** means each wave starts with its least critical members. If a wave runs out of time, you have deferred the least important things, not whichever happened to be alphabetically last.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: ## Applying freeze windows and other constraints

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: The graph gives you a feasible order. Reality gives you a calendar: a retailer cannot touch anything in November, a payroll system cannot move mid-month, a licence expires in March, hardware goes EOL in June.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Do not encode these into the graph. Keep them as a separate filter applied to the computed order, so that when the calendar changes you do not recompute dependencies:

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text:
```python
def schedule(waves, constraints, calendar):
    """Assign dates to waves, deferring any wave whose members are
    frozen in the next available window."""
    plan, cursor = [], calendar.first_window()
    for wave in waves:
        while any(c.blocks(app, cursor) for app in wave for c in constraints):
            cursor = calendar.next_window(cursor)
        plan.append((cursor, wave))
        cursor = calendar.next_window(cursor)
    return plan
```

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Hardware EOL deserves special handling, because it is the one constraint that runs the other way: it is a *deadline*, not a blackout. An application on hardware that dies in June must be in a wave before June, regardless of where the topological order wants to put it. If the order says otherwise, you have found a forced modernization: break the dependency, or accept a hybrid period where that application runs in the cloud while its dependency is still on-prem.

title: Generating a migration wave plan from your CMDB instead of a spreadsheet
text: Finding that in month one instead of month five is the entire return on building this.

text: The output is a plan, and plans are wrong. The value is not the first plan; it is that the second one takes four minutes.

When a team discovers an undeclared dependency in week seven — and they will — the question "what does this do to the plan?" is answered by a commit rather than a workshop.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: # Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: There is a received wisdom about cloud migration that goes roughly: lift and shift is what you do if you lack ambition. You will not get the benefits of the cloud. You will move your problems rather than solve them. Do it properly — refactor, go cloud-native, use managed services.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: I have run migrations both ways and I think this wisdom is mostly wrong, or rather, it is right about a thing that does not matter as much as it claims.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Here is the reframing I would offer: **rehosting is not an architectural choice that happens to be fast. It is a scheduling choice that happens to have architectural consequences.** Once you see it that way, the question stops being "is lift and shift good" — a question with no answer — and becomes "what am I buying with the time, and have I priced what I am deferring".

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## The case against the received wisdom

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: The argument for refactoring during migration is that you are touching the application anyway, so the marginal cost of improving it is low.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: This is true for the code and false for everything else. Here is what actually happens.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Migrating a workload as-is has a *bounded* set of unknowns. The application behaves the same way; what changes is the infrastructure underneath it. When something breaks, the cause is in a short list: networking, identity, storage performance, a hardcoded hostname, a licence check pinned to a MAC address. Painful, but enumerable.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Refactoring during migration has an *unbounded* set of unknowns, because now both the infrastructure and the application have changed. When something breaks, you do not know which half did it. And debugging that question — did the behaviour change because we moved it or because we rewrote it — is where migration schedules go to die. I have watched a two-week cutover become eleven weeks over a single question of that shape.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: There is a second problem, which is organisational. A refactor needs the people who understand the application's business logic. A migration needs the people who understand infrastructure. These are different people, and on a sixty-workload programme you cannot have the first group available for all of it. So the refactoring happens to whichever applications happen to be in the wave when the domain expert is free, which is not a strategy.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## So what are you buying with the time?

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: This is the only question that matters, and it has real answers:

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **An exit from a lease or a contract.** The most common and most legitimate. The data centre contract ends in eleven months. A rehost fits in eleven months; a refactor-everything programme does not. The alternative is not "a better migration" — it is paying for a lease extension, which is a real number you can compare against the cost of deferred modernisation.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Hardware that is going to die.** Storage arrays out of support, a mainframe with no spares, a database version the vendor stopped patching. The deadline is set by physics and procurement, not by you.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **A data-centre event you want to stop fearing.** If you are one UPS failure away from a bad week, getting out fast has a risk value that is hard to put on a slide but is entirely real.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Organisational attention.** This one is underrated. Migrations are funded by a window of executive interest that does not last. A programme that delivers something visible in six months can ask for another six. A programme that delivers its first workload in month nine often does not get asked back.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Those are good reasons, and all four are about time. None of them is about architecture.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## And what are you deferring?

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: The reason lift-and-shift gets a bad reputation is not that it is wrong. It is that the deferred work is almost never scheduled, so "defer" silently becomes "never", and two years later someone writes a blog post about how the cloud did not deliver.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Be specific about the bill you are running up:

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Rightsizing.** Your VMs are sized for a procurement cycle, not for actual load. Expect average utilisation somewhere between 8% and 20%. That is a recurring overpayment starting the day the workload lands.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Managed-service substitution.** A self-managed database on a VM costs you patching, backup verification, failover testing and the engineer-hours to do all three. Some of that is worth keeping. Most is not.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Elasticity you cannot use.** A monolith that scales vertically cannot respond to load by adding instances, so you pay for peak capacity continuously. This is usually the largest single item and the hardest to fix.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Resilience you now pay for differently.** On-prem redundancy was capital already spent. In the cloud, multi-AZ is a recurring charge on every write that crosses a zone. Keeping the on-prem resilience *pattern* in a cloud *pricing model* is one of the quieter cost surprises.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Put numbers on those four, per workload, at planning time. Then the deferral is a financing decision — we are paying X per month extra for Y months in exchange for finishing Z months sooner — rather than an unexamined default.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## The decision rule I would actually use

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Not per programme. Per application, which is the part most programmes get wrong by choosing one strategy for everything.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Rehost when:** the application works, the deadline is external, the business logic is stable, and nobody on the team is frightened of it. Most applications in most estates.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Replatform** (same application, managed database or container runtime underneath) **when:** the operational burden is the main cost and the application does not care where its database lives. This is the highest return-per-unit-risk option available and it is chronically under-used. Moving a self-managed Postgres to a managed one is often a connection-string change and eliminates a whole class of 3am work.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Refactor when:** the application is actively blocking the business, *and* you have the domain expert, *and* the cost shape is bad enough to justify it. Three conditions, all required. Two out of three means wait.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Replace** (buy something) **when:** the capability is not differentiating. Payroll, expenses, CRM, ticketing. The fact that you built it in 2011 is not a reason to keep it.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Retire when:** you can find no user. Run this check properly — it is routine to find 10-20% of an application estate has no meaningful traffic, and every one of those is a workload you do not migrate, test, or pay for. Retiring is the only strategy with a negative cost, and it is the one least likely to have an owner.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: **Retain when:** the thing cannot move for a reason outside your control — latency to a physical process, a regulatory constraint, a vendor licence that forbids virtualisation. Say so explicitly and plan the hybrid rather than discovering it.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: The useful discipline is making this choice per application with a written reason, which is what the 7 Rs framework is for — Pixorama has [the 7 Rs broken down application by application](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) along with how to sequence the resulting mix, which is the harder half.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## The one thing I would not defer

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: If I were setting a single rule, it would be this: **lift and shift the application, never the landing zone.**

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: Rehosting an application is a reversible, bounded compromise. Compromising on identity, account structure, network topology, guardrails and cost attribution is not. Those are the things everything else is built on top of, and retrofitting them means touching every workload you already moved.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: The migrations I have seen fail — genuinely fail, not just cost more than planned — failed because the environment was built in parallel with the first wave under deadline pressure, and it was never governable afterwards. The applications were fine. They were fine in a place nobody could manage.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: So: be as pragmatic as you like about the applications. Be inflexible about the foundation. That asymmetry is, I think, the whole art of it.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: ## Where this leaves the received wisdom

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: "Lift and shift means you won't get cloud benefits" is true and incomplete. You will not get cost or elasticity benefits. You will get out of the data centre, on a deadline, with a bounded risk profile — and if that is what you needed, you got what you paid for.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: The failure mode is not choosing rehost. It is choosing rehost and then not writing down what you deferred, because the deferred list is the entire second half of the project and it has no champion once the migration programme closes and everyone is thanked.

title: Lift and shift is a decision about time, not architecture
text: If the deferred work is genuinely a modernisation question rather than a rightsizing one — if the answer involves changing what the application *is* — then it is worth separating that out as its own decision rather than smuggling it into a migration. The [refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace) question has a different shape and a different cost curve, and migrations that try to answer it mid-flight tend to answer it badly.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: # Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Last issue I claimed that expensive technology surprises are structural decisions showing up late. Migration is the cleanest example, so let me start there.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: I have reviewed a reasonable number of cloud migration business cases. They are not bad documents. The compute forecast is usually within 10%, which for an eighteen-month projection is respectable work.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: They are also missing the same four numbers every time, and those four numbers are what actually determine whether the programme comes in under its run-rate.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## Number one: cross-boundary gigabytes per wave-month

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: During a migration, some of your applications are in the cloud and some are not. Every dependency that spans that boundary generates metered traffic that was previously free, because it ran on a switch you already owned.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The number you want is: **for each dependency, the daily traffic volume multiplied by the number of months its two endpoints will be on opposite sides of the boundary.**

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: You can compute this. Flow logs tell you what talks to what and how much. The wave plan tells you when each thing moves. Join them:

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text:
```
for each dependency (A -> B):
    gb_per_day     = flow_logs[A][B] / 30
    months_split   = abs(wave_of(A) - wave_of(B)) * months_per_wave
    cost           = gb_per_day * 30 * months_split * price_per_gb
```

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: On one programme I was close to, this came out at about $11,000 a month averaged across an eleven-month hybrid period. Budgeted: zero. The information was sitting in flow logs the whole time.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The reason nobody computes it is that it falls between two people. The infrastructure team has the flow logs and does not own the business case. The programme office owns the business case and has never seen a flow log.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: What makes this number worth more than its own size: it is also a **resequencing instruction**. A dependency carrying 80GB/day whose endpoints are six waves apart is telling you to move those two applications together. Every time I have seen this query run, it has changed the wave order.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## Number two: current utilisation of the machines you are about to copy

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Not capacity. Utilisation. Average and p95 CPU and memory, over at least a month, for every VM in scope.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The number is almost always lower than people expect — I have seen estates average 8-20% — and the reason is structural and completely rational. On owned hardware, you size for peak plus growth plus a safety margin, because adding capacity means a purchase order and a six-week lead time. Over-provisioning costs you a one-off capital inefficiency. Under-provisioning costs you an outage you cannot fix quickly.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: In the cloud, that same sizing logic is a recurring monthly charge for capacity you do not use, protecting against a risk that no longer exists.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: So if you rehost as-is, you are copying the machines *and the assumption*. The number tells you how much that costs: the gap between what you are provisioning and what you are using, priced monthly, from the day each wave lands.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: I am not arguing against rehosting. It is frequently correct, and I will defend it in a future issue. I am arguing that the deferral should have a number and a date attached, because "we'll rightsize later" with no number and no owner reliably becomes 11% utilisation a year later.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## Number three: tag coverage, measured not assumed

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: What percentage of your existing infrastructure can be attributed to a specific business owner and cost centre, today, from metadata rather than from someone's memory?

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Measure it. Do not ask whether you have a tagging policy — everyone has a tagging policy. Measure actual coverage.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: In my experience the honest answer is somewhere between 50% and 70%, and the missing portion is not randomly distributed. It is concentrated in things created in a hurry, which is also where the oversized instances and the orphaned volumes are.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Why this number decides the migration: at 60% coverage you cannot have a cost conversation. The invoice arrives as one figure, finance asks why cloud is expensive, and the only available answer is a breakdown by service type — "compute is 40% of the bill" — which no team can act on.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The fix costs one policy change: make the tags mandatory at resource creation, so the resource cannot exist without them. It feels bureaucratic in week one. It is the difference between a cost conversation and an argument, and retro-tagging later is six weeks of archaeology through audit logs.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## Number four: how long your engineering team takes to ship an infrastructure change

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: This is the one nobody thinks belongs in a migration business case, and I now think it is the most predictive of the four.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Measure: from "we agree this change is needed" to "it is in production", for a routine infrastructure change. Median, over the last ten.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: If that number is two days, your migration will go roughly as planned, because when you discover something — and you will discover something every week — you can respond.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: If it is six weeks, the migration will take much longer than the plan says, regardless of how good the plan is. Every discovery becomes a six-week decision, and discoveries are serial because each one changes what you look at next.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: This number is a property of your organisation, not your technology, and it is the one you cannot buy your way out of. A migration programme with excellent tooling and a six-week change cycle will be paced by the six weeks.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The useful consequence: if that number is bad, **fix it before the migration, not during.** Six weeks spent on the deployment pipeline before wave one is recovered several times over. I have watched a team do exactly this and it was the highest-return decision of their programme, though it looked like a delay at the time.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## What the four have in common

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: None of them are about the cloud.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Number one is about your dependency graph. Two is about a procurement cycle from 2017. Three is about governance discipline. Four is about your delivery capability.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: The cloud is where they become visible, because the cloud prices things that were previously free or capital. That is the whole mechanism of the "cloud is more expensive than we thought" conversation: not that the cloud is expensive, but that it meters things your previous environment did not, and the meter is a readout of structure you had never had to look at.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Which is last issue's claim, in a specific setting: the structural decisions were made years ago. The migration just moved them somewhere with a price tag.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: ## If you are about to start one

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Compute one, two and three this week. They are genuinely an afternoon each, and between them they will tell you more about your migration's cost than another month of planning.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Four takes longer because you have to look at your last ten changes honestly, and the answer is often unwelcome.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: Then put all four in the business case as explicit lines, including the ones that make the saving look smaller. A business case that shows a modest saving and survives contact with the invoice is worth considerably more than one that shows a large saving and does not — not least because the second kind damages the credibility of the next programme.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: For the full sequence around all this — the assessment work, choosing a strategy per application rather than per programme, how to build the landing zone before wave one, and what to modernise during the move versus after — my colleagues wrote [the long version of this](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) with the steps laid out properly. The part I would read twice is the assessment phase, because all four of these numbers belong there and it is the phase most programmes compress.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
text: A note if you are running this with a partner rather than in-house: ask which of these four they will compute before the business case is signed. All four are cheap, and a firm that has not offered them is quoting you a migration rather than a result. My colleagues' notes on [how to read a migration firm's partner tiers](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-cloud-migration-companies-india) make a related point I had not thought about until I read it: a provider's top-tier partner badge is a measure of committed spend routed through them, which is not an incentive to make number two smaller.

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration

title: Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
Issue 2: The four numbers that decide a migration
