title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: # Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Every migration business case I have reviewed models compute accurately. Most model storage adequately. Almost none model data movement, and data movement is the line item that turns a 20% saving into a 15% increase.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: The reason is structural. Compute cost is a function of things you chose deliberately — instance sizes, counts, hours. Egress cost is a function of something nobody chose: where the data happens to be relative to where the compute happens to be, which in a migration is decided by wave sequencing rather than by design.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Here is how to find it before the invoice does.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## Why it is invisible in planning

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Pre-migration, all your traffic is on your own network. A service reading 200GB a day from a database two racks away costs nothing marginal — the switch is a capital asset, already paid for.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Post-migration, if that service is in the cloud and the database is still on prem, the same 200GB a day is cross-boundary. At roughly $0.09/GB that is $540/month for one dependency, and the uncomfortable part is that it is *recurring for as long as the hybrid period lasts*, which is always longer than planned.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Multiply across a mid-size estate during a 14-month migration and this is routinely a six-figure line nobody budgeted.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Three distinct charges people conflate:

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text:
| Flow | Typical cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Internet egress | ~$0.05-0.12/GB | Tiered, falls with volume |
| Cross-region | ~$0.02/GB | Both directions in some services |
| Cross-AZ | ~$0.01/GB each way | **Both** directions — easy to double-count |
| Ingress | $0 | Which is why it feels free to move data in |
| NAT gateway processing | ~$0.045/GB | *On top of* egress, and often larger |

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: That last row is the one that surprises people. If your private-subnet workloads reach the internet through a managed NAT gateway, you pay a processing fee per gigabyte *plus* the egress. For high-volume flows the NAT fee can exceed the egress fee. A VPC endpoint for the same service costs a fraction.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Cross-AZ is the quiet one. A three-AZ Kafka cluster with replication factor 3 pays cross-AZ on every replica write, in both directions, forever. That is an architectural choice with a direct monthly number attached, and it is almost never costed at design time.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## Finding it in your own traffic, before you migrate

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: You do not need a tool. You need flow logs and a dependency inventory, and you need to join them.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text:
```sql
-- Flow records, aggregated per application pair per day.
-- The question: for each candidate migration wave, how much traffic
-- crosses the boundary that the wave is about to create?
WITH flows AS (
  SELECT
    src.app_id              AS src_app,
    dst.app_id              AS dst_app,
    SUM(f.bytes) / 1e9      AS gb_per_day
  FROM flow_logs f
  JOIN asset_map src ON f.src_addr = src.ip
  JOIN asset_map dst ON f.dst_addr = dst.ip
  WHERE f.day >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT
  f.src_app,
  f.dst_app,
  ROUND(f.gb_per_day, 1)                       AS gb_per_day,
  w_src.wave                                   AS src_wave,
  w_dst.wave                                   AS dst_wave,
  -- Months of hybrid exposure for this edge
  GREATEST(w_src.wave, w_dst.wave) - LEAST(w_src.wave, w_dst.wave) AS waves_apart,
  ROUND(f.gb_per_day * 30 * 0.09, 0)           AS usd_per_month_if_split
FROM flows f
JOIN wave_plan w_src ON f.src_app = w_src.app_id
JOIN wave_plan w_dst ON f.dst_app = w_dst.app_id
WHERE w_src.wave <> w_dst.wave
  AND f.gb_per_day > 1
ORDER BY usd_per_month_if_split DESC;
```

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: The top twenty rows of that query are your egress forecast. They are also, more usefully, a **resequencing instruction**: an edge carrying 80GB/day whose endpoints are six waves apart is telling you to move those two applications together.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: This is the single highest-return query in migration planning and it takes an afternoon. I have never run it on a real estate without finding at least one pair that should obviously have been in the same wave.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## Data gravity is a design constraint, not a metaphor

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: "Data gravity" sounds like consultant-speak. It describes something concrete: the larger a dataset, the more expensive it is to compute anywhere other than where it lives, so compute migrates toward data rather than the reverse.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Practically, this means the sequencing rule is: **move the data first, or move the data last, but never move the compute separately from the data it reads heavily.**

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: The two workable patterns:

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: **Data first.** Replicate the datastore to the cloud, run it as a read replica during transition, cut over writes when the dependent applications have moved. Costs you an ingress period (free) and dual-running storage (cheap). Avoids sustained egress entirely. This is almost always correct.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: **Data last.** Keep the datastore on prem, move only applications whose read volume is genuinely low. Requires the query above to prove "low" rather than assume it.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: The pattern that does not work, and is the default if you do not decide: move applications in wave order and let the data follow whenever it is convenient. That maximises the number of wave-months where a chatty edge spans the boundary.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## Instrument so attribution is possible

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: If you cannot attribute egress to a workload, you cannot have a conversation about it — the bill arrives as one number and the discussion becomes "cloud is expensive."

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Minimum instrumentation, in place before wave one:

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text:
```hcl
# Every resource carries workload identity. Enforced by policy so the
# resource cannot be created without it — a tagging *request* gets you
# about 60% coverage, which is useless for attribution.
locals {
  required_tags = {
    workload    = var.workload
    env         = var.environment
    owner       = var.owner_email
    cost_centre = var.cost_centre
    data_class  = var.data_classification
  }
}

# VPC flow logs to the central logging account, with the fields you
# actually need for cost work.
resource "aws_flow_log" "workload" {
  log_destination      = var.central_flow_log_arn
  log_destination_type = "s3"
  traffic_type         = "ALL"
  vpc_id               = aws_vpc.workload.id

  # pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr matter: without them, traffic through an
  # intermediary is attributed to the intermediary, not the real endpoints.
  log_format = join(" ", [
    "$${version}", "$${account-id}", "$${vpc-id}", "$${subnet-id}",
    "$${srcaddr}", "$${dstaddr}", "$${srcport}", "$${dstport}",
    "$${protocol}", "$${bytes}", "$${packets}",
    "$${pkt-srcaddr}", "$${pkt-dstaddr}", "$${flow-direction}",
    "$${traffic-path}", "$${start}", "$${end}", "$${action}",
  ])
}
```

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: `pkt-srcaddr` and `pkt-dstaddr` versus `srcaddr`/`dstaddr` is the detail worth knowing: with a NAT gateway or a transit gateway in the path, the plain fields show the intermediary. You will attribute 40% of your egress to "the NAT gateway", which is true and useless.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## The three fixes, in order of return

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: **1. VPC endpoints for provider services.** If workloads reach object storage, queues, or secret stores over the internet via NAT, you are paying NAT processing plus egress for traffic that never needed to leave the provider network. Gateway endpoints for object storage are typically free. This is the single cheapest fix available and it is frequently worth 20-30% of a NAT bill.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: **2. Collapse chatty edges into one AZ or one service.** A cross-AZ call pattern in a request path is paying twice per hop for availability you may not need at that tier. Multi-AZ for the datastore, single-AZ for the stateless tier behind an AZ-aware load balancer, is a legitimate design that many teams reject reflexively.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: **3. Cache at the boundary, not at the service.** A read-through cache in the cloud in front of an on-prem datastore converts sustained egress into a bounded miss rate. During a hybrid period this is often the highest-leverage code change available — one team I worked with cut a $4,100/month cross-boundary bill to about $300 with a cache and a 15-minute TTL, because the data was reference data that changed daily.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: And one anti-fix: do not solve this with a reserved-capacity or committed-spend discount. Commitments reduce the unit price of a structure you have not changed. The structure is the problem — which is the whole argument in [Pixorama wrote this up as an architecture problem wearing a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem), and it matches what I have seen every time: cost programmes that only touch pricing get one good quarter and then revert.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: ## What to do on Monday

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Run the flow-log join. Produce the top twenty cross-boundary edges with a dollar figure. Take that list to whoever owns the wave plan and resequence around the top five.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Then add egress as an explicit line in the business case, derived from that query and the planned hybrid duration, rather than omitted. A business case that shows a smaller saving and survives contact with the invoice is worth more than one that shows a larger saving and does not.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: Flexera's annual [State of the Cloud report](https://info.flexera.com/CM-REPORT-State-of-the-Cloud) survey has put managing cloud spend at or near the top of respondents' concerns for years running, alongside consistently large self-reported waste. The waste is not mostly idle instances. It is structural, and data movement is the largest structural component nobody models.

title: Egress is the cloud bill you didn't model
text: For where this fits in sequencing — and why the assessment phase should include the flow-log work rather than treating it as optimisation to do later — Pixorama's [migration strategy guide](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) puts it in step one, which is the right place for it. And if you are shortlisting partners, their notes on [reading cloud migration firms' partner tiers](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-cloud-migration-companies-india) are a useful corrective: a top-tier badge measures committed spend through that provider, which is close to the opposite of an incentive to reduce your bill.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: # We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The rewrite had a name, a budget, a two-year timeline and eleven people assigned to it. It had a slide deck with a diagram of the target architecture, and the diagram was genuinely good. I had helped make it.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: We cancelled it in week five.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: What we did instead was six months of work so unexciting that it was difficult to report on. At the end of those six months, the system that was going to be replaced was still there, still running the business, and nobody wanted to replace it any more. Not because we had grown fond of it — because the things that had made it intolerable were gone.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: I have thought about this a lot since, because the decision was nearly the other way, and the argument that changed it was not an engineering argument.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ## What was actually wrong

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The system was fourteen years old. Roughly 400,000 lines, a language two versions out of support, a schema with 200 tables and some genuinely alarming design decisions in it. Four people understood it; two of them were close to retirement.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Everyone agreed it had to go. When I asked people *why*, I got these answers:

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text:
1. Changes take too long. A small feature was six to eight weeks.
2. It breaks in production and we cannot tell why.
3. We cannot hire for it.
4. Deployments are a weekend event requiring four people.
5. It is going to fall over one day and we will not be able to fix it.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: That list is what justified the rewrite. And looking at it now, the thing I notice is that **not one of those five items is a statement about the architecture.** They are all statements about the *experience of working on it*.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: That distinction is what the week-five conversation turned on. Someone in a review — not an engineer, our delivery lead — asked a question that I have reused many times since: *if we fixed the five complaints without replacing the system, would we still want to replace it?*

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Nobody could say yes with a straight face.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ## The six months

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: So we took the five complaints as the backlog. In order of how much they were hurting:

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ### Deployments (6 weeks)

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: A weekend deployment needing four people meant we deployed monthly, which meant every release carried a month of changes, which meant every failure was hard to attribute, which meant we were cautious, which meant we deployed monthly.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: We did not change the application. We automated the existing runbook. The runbook was a 40-step Word document; it became a script, then a pipeline. Six weeks, two engineers, no application code modified.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Deployment went from a staffed weekend to eleven minutes on a Tuesday.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: This single change did more for the other four complaints than anything else we did, which I did not expect. Feature lead time dropped before we had touched anything that affects feature lead time, because the batch size collapsed.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ### Observability (7 weeks)

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: "It breaks and we cannot tell why" was literally true: the application logged to local files on each of six servers, with no correlation between them, and the logs were rotated daily.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: We added structured logging with a request ID threaded through the entry points, shipped it centrally, and put up four dashboards and about a dozen alerts. We did not instrument the whole system — we instrumented the eight code paths that generated the most support tickets.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Mean time to diagnose went from "a day and a guess" to minutes for the common cases. Two long-standing intermittent bugs were identified in the first fortnight, because for the first time we could see them happen.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ### The test harness (9 weeks)

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: This was the hardest part and the highest value. There were almost no tests. Any change therefore required manual regression testing, which is where most of the six-to-eight weeks went.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: We did not try to retrofit unit tests across 400,000 lines; that is the project that never finishes. We built a characterisation harness at the boundary: record real requests and responses in production, replay them against a candidate build, diff the outputs.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text:
```
record (prod, 2 weeks of traffic) -> 140,000 request/response pairs
replay (candidate build)          -> diff
```

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: This is a crude technique and it was transformative. It does not tell you the system is correct; it tells you the system has not *changed*, which is the actual question when modifying a legacy system. Within a month, a change that had required six weeks of manual regression could be validated in an afternoon.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: It also found three places where the system's behaviour differed from its documentation, which was educational for everyone who had been planning to rewrite it from the documentation.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ### Modularisation at the seams (10 weeks)

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Only now did we touch the architecture, and only at the edges.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Two capabilities were genuinely separable and genuinely painful: a reporting layer that locked tables during business hours, and a notification system that nobody wanted to be near. We extracted both. New services, new code, clean interfaces, with the characterisation harness proving the old behaviour was preserved.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: That is maybe 8% of the system by line count. It was most of the daily pain.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ### Hiring (ongoing, mostly solved by the above)

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: "We cannot hire for it" turned out to be partly false. We could not hire people excited about a system with no tests, no observability, and weekend deployments — which is a different problem, and we had just fixed it. The language was a smaller obstacle than the working conditions; competent engineers will learn an unfashionable language for a well-run system, and will not join a badly-run one for a fashionable one.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ## What the rewrite would have actually cost

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The two-year estimate was wrong in the way all rewrite estimates are wrong, and I want to be precise about the mechanism rather than just asserting it.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The estimate was built from the *known* requirements — the documented behaviour, the current feature set, the integrations we knew about. That part was probably about right.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: What it omitted:

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: **The undocumented behaviour.** Our characterisation harness found three divergences in the eight code paths we instrumented. Extrapolated across the system, there were hundreds of behaviours nobody had written down, each one load -bearing for some customer, discoverable only by breaking it.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: **The two-system period.** During a rewrite, both systems need maintenance. Every feature request in those two years gets built twice or deferred. The business does not stop for your migration, and the rewrite team's velocity assumption generally pretends it does.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: **The convergence problem.** The old system keeps changing while you rebuild it, so the target keeps moving. Teams solve this by freezing the old system, which the business overrules by month four.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: My honest estimate is three and a half to four years, and a 40% chance of abandonment somewhere in year two — at which point you have the original system plus a half-finished replacement plus a demoralised team.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The six months of boring work cost roughly a tenth of the rewrite's first year and delivered most of what people actually wanted.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ## When the rewrite is right

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: I am not arguing rewrites are never correct. I have seen two that were, and they had a common feature: **the requirements had changed, not just the code.**

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: If what the business needs is now materially different from what the system does, then carefully preserving its existing behaviour is wasted effort — you are spending money to keep something you want to get rid of. That is a genuine rebuild case.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The rewrite that is usually wrong is the one where the requirements are stable and the complaint is that the code is unpleasant. That is a maintainability problem, and maintainability problems have cheaper solutions than replacement.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The question I would put to any rewrite proposal: *what will the new system do that the old one does not?* If the answer is a list of qualities — it will be testable, observable, modular, modern — those are properties you can add to the system you have. If the answer is a list of capabilities the business needs and cannot get, that is a rebuild.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Pixorama's framing of [how to decide between the three](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace) — refactor, rebuild or replace — is a more structured version of the same test, and their broader piece on [legacy application modernization](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization) covers the option space including buying a product, which in our case was genuinely considered and rejected for one capability and accepted for another.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: ## The part that is hard to replicate

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: I will be honest about why this is difficult, because "just do the boring work" is advice that ignores the real obstacle.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: The rewrite was *easier to fund*. It had a narrative, a target architecture diagram, a name, and an end state that sounded like progress. It was a thing you could announce.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: "We are going to spend six months automating the deployment, adding logging and building a replay harness" is not an announcement. It has no end state. Nobody gets promoted for it. The quarterly update is "deployment is faster now", which is unglamorous next to "we are modernising the platform".

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: What made it possible for us was reframing the six months as **a precondition** rather than an alternative. The pitch was not "do this instead of the rewrite". It was: *we cannot safely rewrite this system until we can deploy it, observe it and test it — so we are doing that first, and we will revisit the rewrite in six months with much better information.*

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: That got funded. And six months later, with the information, nobody wanted it.

title: We replaced a rewrite with six months of boring work
text: Which was, I think, always the likely outcome, and is a reasonable way to find out.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: # Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Here is a pattern I have now seen four times, closely enough to be confident about the mechanism.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: A company's cloud bill is uncomfortable. Somebody runs a cost-optimisation programme. Rightsizing, reserved capacity, deleting orphaned volumes, turning non-production environments off overnight, negotiating a committed-spend discount.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: It works. The bill comes down 20-25% in a quarter. There is a slide.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Then over the following two or three quarters it climbs back to roughly where it started, and the second cost-optimisation programme gets a worse reception than the first.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: ## Why the second quarter undoes the first

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Because the first programme fixed consequences, and the causes were untouched.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The things a cost programme typically fixes — oversized instances, idle resources, un-discounted on-demand usage, dev environments running at 3am — are all *symptoms of a structure that keeps producing them*. Delete the orphaned volumes and the process that orphans volumes is still running. Rightsize the instances and the deployment pattern that oversizes them is unchanged.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Meanwhile the actual cost drivers are things like:

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text:
- A messaging cluster replicating across availability zones on every write,
  paying cross-zone charges in both directions, forever.
- A reporting service pulling full table extracts from another service's
  database because there is no event stream, so the same data moves nightly at
  full volume.
- A batch pipeline re-reading the same reference dataset forty times in a single
  run, because each step was written independently and nobody owns the pipeline.
- A service boundary drawn around team ownership rather than data locality, so a
  request path crosses the network four times where it could cross once.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Every one of those is a recurring charge generated by a design decision. Pricing levers reduce the *unit cost* of running them. They do not stop you running them.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: So the saving is real and bounded, and the growth underneath it continues. Hence one good quarter.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: ## The finance dashboard as an architecture readout

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: What I find genuinely interesting about this is the direction of information flow. The finance dashboard is often the **first** place architectural incoherence becomes visible, and it shows up there before it shows up in any engineering metric.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Think about why. A chatty service boundary does not necessarily make latency bad enough to alert on. The nightly full-table extract completes within its window. The over-replicated cluster is perfectly healthy. Nothing is broken. Every dashboard an engineering team looks at is green.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: But each of those is converting a design decision into a monthly charge, so the bill grows in a shape that matches the architecture. The line item called "data transfer" is a measurement of how much your services talk across boundaries. The compute line is a measurement of your scaling model. These are architectural facts, denominated in dollars.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Which means — and this is the part I want to land — **the cost report is observability.** It is lagging, badly labelled, and aggregated by the wrong dimensions, but it contains information about structure that no engineering dashboard contains.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: My colleagues made this argument at more length, calling cloud cost [an architecture problem wearing a finance costume](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-cost-is-an-architecture-problem), which is a better phrase than any I have come up with and matches what I have watched happen.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: ## The gap that makes this hard

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: I do not want to present this as a process failure with a process fix, because the real obstacle is organisational and it is genuinely difficult.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The people who can read the cost shape of an architecture are architects and senior engineers. They are fully occupied with delivery.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The people who own the cost conversation are in finance. They cannot read an architecture, and no dashboard fixes that — giving finance a more detailed breakdown of services they do not understand produces more precise confusion.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The gap between those two groups is where this money goes. And both groups are behaving reasonably: finance is asking the right question in the only vocabulary it has, and engineering is answering a different question because that is the one it was asked.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: What closed it on one programme I was part of — eventually, after about two years of not closing it — was putting one engineer in the monthly finance review with a standing agenda item. Three slides, every month:

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text:
1. The three largest cost drivers this month.
2. The design decision behind each.
3. What changing it would cost in engineering time.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: That is it. No dashboard, no tooling, no FinOps platform. One engineer, three slides, once a month.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: That meeting is where the batch pipeline got its cache and the reporting service got its event stream. Both had been obvious to engineers for over a year. Neither had ever been prioritised, because they were invisible to the people doing the prioritising — there was no feature in them, no incident driving them, and the cost case had never been made in a room where it counted.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: It should have existed in month one. I think it is probably the highest-leverage meeting in any organisation spending meaningfully on cloud, and it costs an hour.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: ## The question that actually works

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: If you take one thing from this issue, take the reframing of the question.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The standard cost question is: **"can we reduce this line item?"** It leads to pricing levers, because that is what it is asking about.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: The better question is: **"why does this line item exist?"**

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Applied to the four examples above, that question produces:

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text:
- *Why do we pay cross-zone transfer on every write?* Because the cluster is
  configured for an availability target nobody has validated against the
  business requirement. Maybe it is correct. Maybe it was a default.
- *Why does the reporting service read the whole table nightly?* Because there is
  no change stream. One is a week of work and removes the charge permanently.
- *Why does the pipeline read the reference data forty times?* Because nobody
  owns the pipeline end to end. A cache and an owner.
- *Why does this request cross the network four times?* Because the service
  boundaries follow the org chart from two reorganisations ago.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: None of those answers is "we need a better discount". Three of the four are a week or two of engineering with a permanent effect, which is a much better return than a commitment discount that locks you into the current structure for three years.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: That last point deserves emphasis, because it is the trap: **a committed-spend discount on a bad structure is worse than no discount.** You have reduced the unit price and simultaneously made it harder to justify changing the thing, because now you have committed capacity to fill.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: ## What I would do with one afternoon

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Take last month's bill. Sort by cost, descending. Take the top five lines.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: For each one, write a single sentence explaining which design decision produces it. Not which service — which *decision*.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: If you can write that sentence for all five, you are in better shape than most organisations I have seen, and you have a prioritised architecture backlog with dollar figures attached, which is the most fundable engineering artefact there is.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: If you cannot write it for three of them, that is the actual finding, and it is usually an attribution problem rather than an understanding problem — which is issue two's third number coming back round.

title: Issue 3: Architecture debt shows up on the finance dashboard first
text: Next issue: the modernisation decision tree, and the rewrite I helped get cancelled.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: # The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Everyone knows the strangler fig pattern. Put a facade in front of the legacy system, route one capability at a time to new code, repeat until the old thing has no traffic, delete it.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The pattern is right. What nobody tells you is that roughly 70% of the work is in three things the diagram does not show: where the routing decision lives, what happens to the data, and how you decide you are finished. Get those wrong and you end up in the failure mode that is genuinely worse than not starting — a permanent two-system estate where every feature has to be built twice.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: I have been through this four times. Here is what the diagram leaves out.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ## The routing layer is a product, not a config file

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The naive version: nginx with a growing list of path rules.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: It breaks the first time a migration is not clean along a path boundary — which is the first time, because legacy systems are not organised by URL. You will need to route on things like:

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text:
- **Tenant.** Migrate customer by customer, not endpoint by endpoint. Far lower
  risk, because a bug affects one tenant.
- **Percentage.** Ramp 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% on a single endpoint.
- **Request shape.** `GET /api/invoices` to the new service, `POST` still
  legacy, because reads are safe and writes are not.
- **A manual kill switch** that does not require a deploy.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: That is four orthogonal dimensions, which means the routing decision is a function, not a table:

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The stable hash is the detail I would underline. A naive `random() < 0.05` means the same tenant hits the new service on one request and the legacy one on the next. If the two have any state divergence at all — and they do — you get intermittent, unreproducible bugs that cost a fortnight to diagnose.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Keep the flags in a store you can change without deploying, and make the kill switch a single call that forces every rule to `LEGACY`. You will use it. The first time you use it, the fact that it takes 20 seconds rather than a 40-minute rollback deploy is the entire justification for building it.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ## The data problem, which is the actual problem

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Routing reads is easy. The hard question is what owns the data.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Three options, in increasing order of both difficulty and value:

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ### Option A: new service reads the legacy database

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Fastest to ship. The new service is a read-model over the legacy schema.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text:
```
[client] -> [router] -> [new-invoices] -> (reads) -> [legacy DB]
                     -> [legacy app]    -> (writes) -> [legacy DB]
```

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Honest assessment: this is not modernization, it is a new UI. You have not decoupled anything — the legacy schema is still the contract, and you cannot delete the legacy system because it still owns writes. Useful as a first step to build confidence. Dangerous if you stop here, because it *feels* like progress and it is a dead end.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ### Option B: dual write, legacy is source of truth

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The new service writes to its own store and to the legacy one. Legacy stays authoritative. Reads can come from either, and you compare them.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text:
```python
def create_invoice(payload):
    legacy_result = legacy_client.create_invoice(payload)   # authoritative
    try:
        new_store.upsert(from_legacy(legacy_result))
    except Exception:
        # Never fail the request because the shadow write failed.
        metrics.increment("shadow_write.failure")
        log.exception("shadow write failed", invoice=legacy_result.id)
    return legacy_result
```

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The point of this phase is not the writes — it is the **comparison**. Run the new read path in shadow mode: serve the legacy answer, compute the new answer, diff them, log the mismatches, serve nothing from the new path.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Run this for weeks. The mismatch rate is your readiness metric, and it will be appalling at first — in one case we started at 11% and spent five weeks getting to 0.02%, and every one of those mismatches was a real behaviour in the legacy system that nobody had documented. Rounding on partial refunds. A timezone assumption in a date field. A status that could be `NULL` only for records created before 2019.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: **This is where the value of the whole exercise is.** The shadow comparison is how you discover the actual specification. Skip it and you ship a new service that is correct according to the requirements and wrong according to the business.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ### Option C: new service owns the data

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Cut over writes. Legacy reads from the new service, or gets a feed, or is decommissioned for that capability.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Only go here when the mismatch rate is near zero and stays there under a full business cycle — which for most domains means a month-end, and for some means a year-end.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ## Exit criteria, decided in advance

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Here is the failure mode that actually kills these programmes. Not technical failure. Stalling.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: You migrate the three easy capabilities, the ones with clean boundaries and low risk. Momentum is great, the demo is impressive. Then you reach the capability that touches everything — usually pricing, entitlements or whatever the equivalent of "the billing engine" is in your domain. It is 40% of the monolith's logic, it has no clean boundary, and the business case for migrating it is weak because it works.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: So it doesn't get migrated. And now you have two systems forever. Every feature is built twice, every incident is diagnosed in two places, and the team that owns the legacy system cannot be disbanded. The total cost of this steady state is higher than either finishing or never starting.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Avoid it by writing down, before the first route is moved:

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text:
1. **The full capability inventory**, including the horrible one. If you cannot
   name an approach for the horrible one, you are not ready to start — you are
   planning to build a permanent hybrid and should decide that explicitly.
2. **A decommission date for the legacy system**, in the programme plan, with a
   named owner. Not "when migration completes". A date.
3. **A rule that the legacy system takes no new features** from day one.
   This is the one that gets violated, and every violation extends the
   endgame.
4. **The sequence ending with the hardest capability, not beginning with it** —
   but with the hardest one's approach designed first. Build confidence on easy
   wins, but design for the hard case, or your facade will not support it.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: On point 4: if the horrible capability needs request-shape routing and tenant-level data partitioning, build the facade with those from the start. A routing layer designed for three clean path-based migrations will need to be rebuilt for the fourth, and rebuilding the facade mid-programme is where schedules die.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: ## When not to do this

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Strangler fig is the right answer when the legacy system is large, works, and carries business knowledge nobody has written down. It is the wrong answer when:

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text:
- **The system is small.** Under maybe 30k lines of comprehensible code, a
  rewrite with a shadow-compare period is cheaper than the facade.
- **You are replacing it with a commercial product.** Then the question is data
  migration and process change, not routing.
- **The business logic genuinely is obsolete.** If the requirements have changed
  such that you do not want the legacy behaviour, preserving it through careful
  shadow comparison is wasted effort. Rebuild.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: That decision — whether this is a refactor, a rebuild or a replace — is upstream of everything in this post, and getting it wrong means executing a pattern beautifully in service of the wrong strategy. Pixorama's write-up on [refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace) is a reasonable framework for making it, and they have [the modernization options laid out](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-application-modernization) with the trade-offs for each.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: Martin Fowler's [original write-up of the pattern](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/StranglerFigApplication.html) remains the clearest statement of why it works, and is short.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: One practical note on staffing this: the shadow-comparison phase needs people who will sit with a 0.02% mismatch rate for five weeks rather than declare victory at 2%. That is a temperament more than a skill set, and it is worth testing for explicitly if you are bringing in a firm — Pixorama's [comparison of custom software firms in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-software-development-companies-india) is unusual in disclosing that they are one of the ten listed, which at least tells you what you are reading.

title: The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
The strangler fig in practice: routing traffic off a monolith without a rewrite
text: The summary I would give a team starting this on Monday: the pattern is not the hard part, and the new services are not the hard part. Build the routing layer as a real product with a kill switch and stable per-tenant hashing. Spend disproportionate time in shadow comparison, because that is where you learn what the system actually does. And write the decommission date down before you start, because the only version of this that fails is the one that never ends.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: # Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: I have been close to four agent builds in the last eighteen months. Three of them should not have been agents. One of them genuinely needed to be, and the difference between those two categories turns out to be sharp, cheap to test for, and almost never tested for.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The three that should not have been agents all shipped. They all work. They all cost between four and nine times what the non-agent version would have cost, and two of them are less reliable than a state machine would have been. That is the expensive kind of success.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## The test

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Here is the question I now ask first, before any discussion of frameworks, models or tools:

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **Can you draw the decision tree?**

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Not "is it complicated". Not "does it have many branches". Just: if you sat down with a domain expert and enough patience, could you enumerate the decision points and what determines each one?

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: If yes, you have a workflow. Write the workflow. You may well want a model *inside* it — for classification, extraction, summarisation, generation — but the control flow belongs in code, where it is deterministic, testable, debuggable and cheap.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: If genuinely no — if the sequence of steps depends on what you discover while doing it, in a way you cannot enumerate in advance — then you need something that decides at runtime, and that is an agent.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: That is the whole test. It takes an afternoon with a whiteboard and it would have saved three projects a lot of money.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## The three that failed the test

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ### The invoice processor

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Brief: "an agent that handles incoming supplier invoices."

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: What it actually needed to do: extract fields from a PDF, match the purchase order, check the amount against tolerance, route exceptions to the right approver, post to the ledger.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: That is five steps in a fixed order. Every branch is enumerable: match found or not, within tolerance or not, approver available or not. The *extraction* step benefits enormously from a model — PDFs from 400 suppliers in 400 layouts is exactly what models are good at. The *control flow* is a flowchart somebody in accounts payable drew in 2019.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Built as an agent, it was non-deterministic in a domain where the auditors require you to explain why a specific invoice was routed to a specific person. "The model decided" is not an acceptable answer in a controls review, and we spent six weeks building trace tooling to reconstruct decisions that a `switch` statement would have made legible for free.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The right shape: deterministic pipeline, model called twice (extraction, and a fuzzy supplier-name match), every branch in code.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ### The onboarding assistant

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Brief: "an agent that onboards new customers."

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Reality: a sequence of document collections with conditional requirements based on entity type and jurisdiction. Complicated — a decision table with about 90 rows. Not unknowable; the compliance team maintained that table in a spreadsheet.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: We built an agent that read the policy documents and reasoned about which documents were required. It was right about 92% of the time.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The spreadsheet was right 100% of the time, because it *was* the policy.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: This is the failure mode I find most painful: using a probabilistic system to approximate a deterministic rule that already exists in written form. The agent was doing lossy compression of a lookup table.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The right shape: the decision table, in code, generated from the compliance team's spreadsheet. Model used for one thing — reading an uploaded document and telling you whether it is the type of document it claims to be, which is a real perception problem.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ### The internal support bot

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Brief: "an agent that answers employee IT questions and takes actions."

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The answering part was a retrieval problem and worked well. The *taking actions* part was where the agent framing caused damage: password resets, access requests, software installs, each with an approval rule.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: As an agent, it occasionally chained actions in ways nobody intended — granting an access request as a step toward resolving a different ticket, which is technically helpful and a security incident.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The right shape: retrieval for answering, and a fixed catalogue of actions each gated by its own deterministic approval rule. The model proposes; code decides.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## The one that passed

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: A diagnostic assistant for a field-service operation. An engineer arrives at a piece of industrial equipment that is not working. They describe symptoms. The system helps them diagnose it.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Why this one genuinely needs an agent:

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **The next step depends on what the previous step revealed, and the space is not enumerable.** The equipment has thousands of failure modes, many in combination. "Check the pressure reading" is the right next action only if the earlier symptoms point there, and the number of symptom combinations is combinatorial rather than listable.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **The information sources are heterogeneous and the right one is not known in advance.** Manuals, past tickets, telemetry, parts inventory, an engineer's free-text note from 2019. Which to consult depends on the hypothesis currently being tested.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **The human is in the loop continuously.** The engineer is standing in front of the machine, providing observations and overriding bad suggestions. The cost of a wrong suggestion is low — the engineer says "no, that's not it" — and the cost of a right suggestion is high.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **There is no existing decision tree, and the attempt to build one had already failed.** They had tried, twice, with a rules engine. The tree was unmaintainable within a year both times.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: That is an agent. And notice the shape of it: **exploratory, human-supervised, cheap-to-be-wrong, heterogeneous tools, genuinely unenumerable.** Those five properties together are rare, and when they are all present the agent framing is not just acceptable but clearly correct.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## Why the costume gets worn

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: I do not think people are being stupid. Three forces push toward agents:

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **The demo is seductive and the hard part is invisible.** An agent that handles one happy-path case takes an afternoon. The control plane that makes it safe — budgets, loop detection, tool tiering, traces, evaluation — is roughly ten times the loop itself, and none of it is visible in the demo.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **"Agent" is how the work gets funded.** A proposal to build a workflow with a model in two steps competes for budget against a proposal to build an AI agent. The second one wins, even when it is the same project described differently and worse.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: **The framework encourages it.** Agent frameworks make the loop trivial and the deterministic alternative feel like a step backwards. If the easiest thing to build is a loop, people build a loop.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## The hybrid that is usually right

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The honest answer for most business problems is not agent-or-workflow. It is a deterministic workflow with model calls at the perception and generation steps:

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text:
```
[intake] -> (model: extract)  -> [validate] -> [branch on rules]
                                                     |
                              +----------------------+
                              |                      |
                        [happy path]           [exception path]
                              |                      |
                      (model: draft reply)     [human review]
                              |                      |
                          [send]                 [resolve]
```

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: Everything in square brackets is code. Everything in parentheses is a model call. The model does perception and language; the code does decisions.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: This architecture is dull and it has properties that matter: every path is testable, every decision is explainable to an auditor, the cost per transaction is predictable, failures are attributable to a specific step, and you can change the business rules without re-evaluating a prompt.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: And when a genuine agent is needed, **put it inside one step of this workflow**, not around the whole thing. The diagnostic assistant above is an agent that lives inside a service-ticket workflow — the ticket lifecycle is deterministic, the diagnosis step is agentic. That containment is what makes it operable.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: ## What I would ask before approving one

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text:
1. **Draw the decision tree.** If it can be drawn, build it.
2. **Does a written rule already exist?** A policy document, a decision table, a
   runbook. If so, encode it; do not ask a model to infer it.
3. **What is the cost of a wrong action?** If it is high, the model proposes and
   code or a human decides. Always.
4. **Is a human in the loop continuously, or only at the end?** Continuous
   supervision makes agents much safer and much more likely to be the right
   choice.
5. **Who is on call for it?** An agent's failure modes are statistical. If there
   is no plan for traces, golden sets and regression gates, the project is not
   ready regardless of its architecture.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: If you are at the stage of scoping this, Pixorama's survey of [fifteen things companies are actually doing with agents right now](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases) is a decent calibration exercise — what strikes me reading it is how narrow the successful deployments are compared to how they get pitched internally. And their walkthrough of [how to build one](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-agent) is a reasonable starting point once you have established that you should.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: If you are buying this rather than building it, the five questions above are the ones to put to an agency, and "draw me the decision tree for our use case" is the single most informative thing you can ask in a sales meeting. A firm that draws it has just told you the work is a workflow and quoted you for an agent. Their guide to [choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c) covers the builder-versus-reseller distinction, which is the same distinction from the buyer's side.

title: Most AI agent projects are workflow projects wearing a costume
text: The claim I would defend: the most valuable thing you can do on an agent project is spend one afternoon trying to draw the decision tree, specifically hoping to succeed. Three times out of four you will, and you will have saved yourself a year.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: # Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: A rewrite I had helped design got cancelled in week five. Eleven people, two years, a target architecture diagram I was proud of.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: What we did instead was six months of work so dull it was hard to report on, at the end of which nobody wanted the rewrite any more. Not because we had grown fond of the old system — because the things that made it intolerable were gone.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: The question that cancelled it came from our delivery lead, not an engineer, and I have used it on every modernisation conversation since:

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text:
> *If we fixed the complaints without replacing the system, would we still want
> to replace it?*

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Nobody could say yes with a straight face.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Here is the tree that question sits inside. Five questions, in order. Order matters — most of the value is in not reaching question five.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Question 1: What are the actual complaints, stated as experiences?

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Not "the architecture is bad". Not "it's legacy". Write down what people say when they complain, in their words.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: On ours, the list was:

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text:
1. Changes take six to eight weeks.
2. It breaks in production and we cannot tell why.
3. We cannot hire for it.
4. Deployments are a weekend event needing four people.
5. It will fall over one day and we will not be able to fix it.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Look at that list. **Not one item is a statement about the architecture.** They are all statements about the experience of working on it.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: That is the usual result, and it is the single most important thing this question reveals. "Legacy" is overwhelmingly a description of working conditions, not of design. And working conditions have much cheaper fixes than replacement.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: If your list does contain genuine architectural statements — "we cannot add a second currency because the schema assumes one", "we cannot serve customers in another region because of a single-datacentre assumption" — those are real and they move you down the tree. But check first, because the architectural framing is the default vocabulary and it is usually imported.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Question 2: Which complaints are fixable without replacement?

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: This is where most systems stop, and it is worth being systematic because the answer is "more than you think".

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Against our five:

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **Deployments** → automate the existing runbook. Six weeks, two engineers, zero application changes. Weekend event became eleven minutes on a Tuesday.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: That one change improved three of the other four complaints, which I did not predict. Feature lead time dropped before we touched anything that affects feature lead time, because deploying monthly meant every release carried a month of changes, which made every failure hard to attribute, which made us cautious, which made us deploy monthly. Breaking that loop was worth more than anything else we did.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **Observability** → structured logging with a request ID, shipped centrally, dashboards and alerts on the eight code paths generating the most support tickets. Seven weeks. Diagnosis went from a day and a guess to minutes.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **Testing** → this was the hard one. No tests, so every change needed manual regression. We did not retrofit unit tests across 400,000 lines; that project never finishes. We built a characterisation harness: record real production traffic, replay it against a candidate build, diff the output.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: It does not tell you the system is correct. It tells you the system has not *changed*, which is the actual question when modifying something legacy. Nine weeks, and it converted a six-week change into an afternoon's validation.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **Hiring** → turned out to be partly downstream of the above. We could not hire people excited about a system with no tests, no observability and weekend deployments. The unfashionable language was a smaller obstacle than the working conditions. Competent engineers will learn an old language for a well-run system and will not join a badly-run one for a fashionable one.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **Will fall over one day** → this is a resilience question, answerable with backup verification, a tested restore and a documented failover, none of which require replacement.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Four and a half of five complaints, fixed in six months, for roughly a tenth of the rewrite's first year.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Question 3: Have the requirements changed, or only the code's condition?

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: This is the actual dividing line, and I think it is the one question that reliably separates a justified rebuild from an unjustified one.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **If the requirements are stable and the complaint is that the code is unpleasant**, that is a maintainability problem. Maintainability problems have cheaper solutions than replacement, which is questions one and two.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: **If what the business now needs is materially different from what the system does**, then carefully preserving its existing behaviour is wasted money. You would be spending two years faithfully reproducing something you want to get rid of.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: That second case is a genuine rebuild, and I have seen two of them. Both involved a business model change — in one case moving from one-off sales to subscriptions, which touched every assumption in the data model and was not reachable by refactoring.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: The useful test: *what will the new system do that the old one does not?* If the answer is a list of qualities — testable, observable, modular, modern — those are properties you can add to what you have. If it is a list of capabilities the business needs and cannot get, you have a rebuild.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Question 4: Is this capability differentiating?

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Before building anything, ask whether you should be building it.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Payroll, expenses, CRM, ticketing, document management, scheduling. The fact that you built it in 2011 because nothing suitable existed is not a reason to rebuild it in 2026, when the market has twenty options.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: This question gets skipped because it is uncomfortable — it implies the last fifteen years of work on that system was a detour — and because the people best placed to evaluate the system are the people who built it.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Get someone else to answer it.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Question 5: Only now, how?

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: If you have reached here, you have established that the complaints are not fixable in place, the requirements have genuinely changed, and the capability is differentiating.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Now the mechanics matter: incremental replacement behind a facade, parallel build with a cutover, or capability-by-capability extraction. These have real trade-offs and they are the subject of most writing about modernisation, which is why I have left them last — the writing concentrates on question five and the decisions are mostly made at questions two and three.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: My colleagues have a structured version of this whole tree as [refactor, rebuild or replace](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/legacy-modernization-refactor-rebuild-replace), which covers the question-five mechanics properly along with the trade-offs for each path. It is the better reference if you have genuinely got to that point.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: ## Why the boring work is hard to choose

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: I want to be honest about the obstacle, because "just do the boring work" ignores why people do not.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: The rewrite was **easier to fund.** It had a name, a diagram, an end state, and a narrative. It was a thing you could announce to a board.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: "We are going to spend six months automating deployment, adding logging and building a replay harness" is not an announcement. It has no end state. Nobody is promoted for it. The quarterly update is "deployment is faster now", which reads as maintenance next to "we are modernising the platform".

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: What made it fundable for us was reframing the six months as a **precondition** rather than an alternative:

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text:
> *We cannot safely rewrite this system until we can deploy it, observe it and
> test it. So we are doing that first, and we will revisit the rewrite in six
> months with much better information.*

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Nobody can argue with that. And six months later, with the information, the rewrite was no longer attractive — which was, I suspect, always the likely outcome, and is a perfectly respectable way to find out.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: If you are facing one of these, that framing is the practical gift of this issue. You do not have to win the argument against the rewrite. You only have to establish that the rewrite should happen *after* the system is deployable, observable and testable. Then let the six months make the argument for you.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: If you want to buy the six months rather than staff it, be precise about what you are buying, because "modernisation" as a service offering usually means question five. The work in question two — deployment automation, structured logging, a characterisation harness — is a [DevOps consulting engagement](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india) and it is a different purchase with a different and much smaller price. Asking for the second when a vendor is selling the first is the whole negotiation.

title: Issue 4: The modernisation decision tree I actually use
text: Next issue: where AI agents earn their keep, which is the one I am most likely to be wrong about.
