title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: # Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: The RAG demo works. Two hundred documents, embeddings in a vector store, top-k of 5, and the answers are good enough that someone says the word "production".

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Then the corpus goes to 10,000 documents and quality falls off a cliff. Not gracefully — the answers get confidently wrong, which is worse than getting worse.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: The instinct is to blame the vector store or reach for a bigger embedding model. Usually neither is the problem. Three things break, in this order.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: ## Failure 1: your chunks lost their context

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Here is the chunking everyone starts with:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
```python
def chunk(text, size=1000, overlap=200):
    chunks, start = [], 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + size])
        start += size - overlap
    return chunks
```

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: At 200 documents this is fine, because the corpus is narrow enough that a semantically vague chunk still retrieves against the right query. At 10,000 it fails, and the reason is worth being precise about.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Consider a chunk from the middle of a policy document:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
> "...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days. In those cases the holder must re-verify before any withdrawal is
> processed. Exceptions require approval from the regional compliance lead..."

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Embed that. What is it about? It has no subject. "This" refers to something 1,400 characters earlier, in a different chunk. The document title, the section, the product it applies to — all absent.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: At 200 documents, a query like *"what happens to dormant accounts"* retrieves it anyway, because nothing else in the corpus mentions dormancy. At 10,000 documents there are 340 chunks mentioning dormancy across 60 products, and this one has no signal to distinguish it from the other 339.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: **The fix is to put the context into the chunk before embedding it.**

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
```python
def contextual_chunk(doc, chunk_text, section_path):
    """Prepend document and section context. The retrieval target is the
    enriched text; the text handed to the model can be either, but the
    enriched version usually reads better in the prompt too."""
    header = " > ".join(filter(None, [
        doc.title,
        doc.product,
        *section_path,
    ]))
    return f"[{header}]\n\n{chunk_text}"
```

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: So the chunk above becomes:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
> "[Retail Savings Terms v4 > Personal Saver > Withdrawals > Dormancy]
>
> ...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days..."

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: That single change has, in my experience, been worth more than every other retrieval improvement combined. Anthropic published [measurements on exactly this](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) — generating a short context sentence per chunk with a cheap model and prepending it, which is the same idea with a generation step instead of structural metadata. Both work; structural metadata is free if you have it, and you usually do.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: **Chunk on structure, not character count.** Markdown headings, HTML sections, PDF bookmarks, docx heading styles. A chunk that is one semantic unit retrieves far better than a chunk that is exactly 1,000 characters ending mid-sentence:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: ## Failure 2: top-k is the wrong retrieval primitive at scale

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: `top_k=5` means "always return 5 things, regardless of whether any of them are relevant." At 200 documents the 5 nearest neighbours are nearly always on-topic. At 10,000 they include three things that are superficially similar and wrong.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: And the model will use them. That is the confidently-wrong failure: the model was handed irrelevant context and had no way to know it was irrelevant, so it synthesised an answer from it.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Two changes:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: **Retrieve wide, then rerank.** Vector similarity is a cheap approximation of relevance. Use it as a filter, not a ranking.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
```python
def retrieve(query, k_final=5):
    # Cast a much wider net than you intend to use
    candidates = vector_store.search(query, k=50)

    # Cross-encoder reranking: slower per item, dramatically more accurate,
    # because it sees query and document together rather than comparing
    # two independently-computed vectors.
    scored = reranker.score(query, [c.text for c in candidates])

    ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scored), key=lambda x: -x[1])
    return [c for c, s in ranked[:k_final] if s > RELEVANCE_FLOOR]
```

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Note the `RELEVANCE_FLOOR`. This is the part people skip, and it is the difference between a system that says "I don't know" and one that invents an answer. **Returning fewer than k results is a feature.** Returning zero and telling the user you found nothing is a feature.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: **Hybrid search, because embeddings are bad at exact tokens.** Dense vectors are excellent at "documents about dormant accounts" and poor at "document reference POL-4471-B" or "section 14.2(c)" or a product name the embedding model has never seen. Run BM25 alongside and fuse:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: RRF needs no score normalisation between the two systems, which is why it beats weighted-sum fusion in practice — you do not have to tune a weight that drifts every time you change embedding models.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: ## Failure 3: you have no way to know it broke

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: The thing that makes this failure mode expensive is not that it happens. It is that nobody notices for six weeks, because the system produces fluent answers throughout.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: You need a golden set. Thirty to a hundred real questions with known-correct source chunks, assembled from actual user queries, and run on every change:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
```python
def evaluate(golden_set):
    """Retrieval metrics only. Deliberately not answer quality — if
    retrieval is wrong the answer cannot be right, and retrieval
    metrics are cheap, deterministic and debuggable."""
    recall_at_k, mrr = [], []
    for case in golden_set:
        retrieved = [c.id for c in retrieve(case.query, k_final=5)]
        hit = set(retrieved) & set(case.expected_chunk_ids)
        recall_at_k.append(1.0 if hit else 0.0)
        rank = next(
            (i for i, cid in enumerate(retrieved, 1)
             if cid in case.expected_chunk_ids),
            None,
        )
        mrr.append(1.0 / rank if rank else 0.0)

    return {
        "recall@5": sum(recall_at_k) / len(recall_at_k),
        "mrr@5":    sum(mrr) / len(mrr),
        "n":        len(golden_set),
    }
```

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Gate deploys on this. A chunking change that improves one query class and destroys another is invisible without it, and chunking changes do that constantly.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: The golden set is tedious to build and it is the highest-return two days of work in the entire project. Build it from real queries — questions you invent are systematically easier than questions users ask, because you unconsciously phrase them using the corpus's own vocabulary.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: ## The order to fix things in

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: If quality has fallen apart at scale, in order:

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text:
1. **Add structural context to chunks.** Biggest single win, lowest effort.
2. **Chunk on document structure** rather than character windows.
3. **Retrieve 50, rerank to 5, with a relevance floor.** Second biggest win.
4. **Add BM25 and fuse with RRF.** Fixes the exact-token blind spot.
5. **Build the golden set.** Do this first if you have the time, because
   without it you cannot tell whether 1-4 helped.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: Things that are usually *not* the problem, despite being where people start: the vector database choice, the embedding model, the chunk size parameter, and the LLM. Swapping a vector store rarely moves retrieval quality, because they are all computing approximately the same nearest neighbours.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: For the conceptual grounding — what retrieval is doing and why it beats retraining for most business use cases — Pixorama has a readable explanation of [what RAG actually is](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-rag-in-ai), and if you are still at the stage of deciding your approach, their [RAG vs fine-tuning](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning) comparison frames the choice usefully: retrieval for knowledge that changes, fine-tuning for behaviour that needs to change. If you are buying this work in rather than building it, their round-up of [AI development firms in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/top-ai-development-companies-india) is a starting point — and the question I would put to any of them is how they measure retrieval quality, because a firm with no answer has not built one of these at scale.

title: Why your RAG retrieval breaks at 10,000 documents
text: The uncomfortable summary: RAG systems do not degrade gracefully with corpus size, and the demo-to-production gap is almost entirely chunking and ranking. If your 200-document prototype is good, you have learned that the plumbing works. You have not yet learned anything about whether the retrieval does.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: # RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: It comes up in week one, every time. Someone has read that there are two approaches to making a language model work on your data, and they want to know which one the project is going to use, so it can go on the architecture slide.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: The honest answer is "neither, probably, and certainly not yet", and the reason is that the question assumes a problem shape that most projects do not have.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## What the two things actually do

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Worth being precise, because the question is usually asked with a slightly wrong model of both.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **Retrieval augments the model's *knowledge*.** At inference time you find relevant documents and put them in the prompt. The model's behaviour does not change; its available facts do. Knowledge updates the moment you update the documents.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **Fine-tuning changes the model's *behaviour*.** You train on examples, and the model learns a format, a tone, a task structure, a classification scheme. It is poor at learning facts — you can teach a model that your return policy is 30 days and it will reproduce that with roughly the reliability of a half-remembered fact, which is to say, not reliably enough for a policy.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: So the actual distinction is **knowledge versus behaviour**, and framed that way the question answers itself in most cases: if your problem is "the model does not know our stuff", that is retrieval. If your problem is "the model does not do the task in the right shape", that is fine-tuning. These are rarely the same problem and they are not alternatives.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: But that still is not the first question.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## The first question

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **What does the correct output look like, and who decides?**

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: This sounds trivially simple and it is where projects fail. Not at the model layer — at the specification layer.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: A worked example. A client wanted an assistant that answered customer questions about their products. Reasonable. We asked for fifty real questions with correct answers.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: It took eleven weeks to get them.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Not because anyone was slow. Because:

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text:
- Support, sales and the product team disagreed about correct answers to about a
  third of the questions.
- Several correct answers depended on the customer's contract, which meant the
  "correct answer" was a function, not a string.
- Four questions had answers that were correct but the legal team would not
  approve in writing.
- Six had no answer anywhere in the company; support staff improvised, and the
  improvisations were inconsistent and mostly fine.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: By the time we had the fifty questions, the project had changed shape entirely. About 40% of the value turned out to be in the *forcing function* — the company now had agreed answers to its fifty most common questions, which it had not had before, and which made the support team measurably better regardless of the AI.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: And the technical approach had become obvious: retrieval over the newly-written canonical answers, no fine-tuning, with contract-dependent questions routed to a deterministic lookup because they were not a language problem at all.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: We could not have chosen that architecture in week one. Nobody could have. The information required to choose it did not exist.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## Why the question gets asked anyway

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Three reasons, all structural rather than foolish:

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **It is the only question with two named answers.** "RAG or fine-tuning" is tractable. "What does correct look like" is an open-ended organisational question that implicates several departments. People reach for the tractable one.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **It feels like an architecture decision, and architecture decisions are supposed to come first.** But this is not architecture; it is implementation detail. The architecture decision is what the system is for and what it is allowed to do.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **Vendors ask it.** If you are evaluating platforms, they ask which approach you need, because their product is better at one. That pushes the question earlier than it belongs.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## The sequence I would actually follow

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **1. Write down fifty real inputs and their correct outputs.** Real ones, harvested from what users actually ask — not invented, because invented examples are systematically easier and use your own internal vocabulary.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Expect this to be hard, slow and politically awkward. That difficulty is information: it tells you the specification does not exist, and no model choice compensates for that.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **2. Notice what the disagreements are about.** This is the highest-value output of step one. Disagreements fall into categories:

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text:
- *We never decided* → you have a policy gap, and the AI project just found it
- *It depends on the customer* → deterministic lookup, not a language problem
- *Legal will not approve a written answer* → out of scope, route to a human
- *Genuinely ambiguous* → the system must be allowed to say so

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Each category has a different solution and only one of them is a model problem.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **3. Now classify what remains.** With the fifty cases in hand, the technical question is finally answerable:

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text:
- Outputs require facts from your corpus → retrieval
- Outputs require a consistent non-obvious structure or style → fine-tuning,
  possibly
- Outputs require multi-step work whose steps vary → an agent, maybe
- Outputs are a deterministic function of structured inputs → **not AI**. Write
  the function.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: In my experience the split lands around: 60% retrieval, 25% not-AI-at-all, 10% agent-shaped, 5% genuine fine-tuning candidates. The 25% is the surprising one and it is pure profit — the cheapest, most reliable part of the system is the part you did not build with a model.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **4. Build the evaluation before the system.** Your fifty cases are now a test suite. This is the thing that makes every later decision empirical instead of argumentative.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: **5. Then pick retrieval or fine-tuning**, and discover that it was not a difficult decision once steps one to four were done.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## When fine-tuning is genuinely right

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: To be fair to it, since I have been dismissive. Fine-tuning earns its place when:

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text:
- You need a **consistent output format** that is awkward to prompt reliably — a
  specific JSON shape, a house style, a classification into forty categories
  with subtle boundaries.
- You have **thousands of examples** of the task being done correctly, as a
  natural by-product of existing work. Not examples you would have to create.
- **Latency or cost** matters enough that a smaller fine-tuned model beating a
  large prompted one is worth the training pipeline.
- The task is **narrow and stable**. Fine-tuning a model for something whose
  definition changes quarterly means retraining quarterly.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Classification and extraction at volume are the strongest cases. Question answering over changing documents is the weakest, and is the thing people most often propose fine-tuning for.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: The trap worth naming: **fine-tuning does not fix hallucination.** It is frequently proposed as a solution to it, on the theory that training on correct facts produces correct facts. It does not; it produces a model that is more confident in the vicinity of those facts, which is worse. Hallucination is addressed by grounding the answer in retrieved text and by letting the system decline to answer.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: Pixorama's [RAG vs fine-tuning in 2026](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-vs-fine-tuning) comparison is a fair treatment of the trade-off if you have reached step five and genuinely need to choose. The thing I would add to any such comparison is that the answer is "both, eventually, for different parts of the system" more often than it is either one.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: ## The uncomfortable conclusion

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: The most useful AI projects I have been near spent their first month not doing AI. They spent it establishing what correct means, which revealed that a quarter of the scope was a deterministic rules problem, a quarter was an organisational policy gap, and the remaining half was a well-specified retrieval problem.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: The projects that started with the architecture question spent their first month building a system and their next six discovering what it should have done.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: And once you are into retrieval, the failure modes are entirely about corpus quality, chunking and ranking rather than model choice — Pixorama's [retrieval that survives contact with real users](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-that-survives-contact-with-users) is about that second phase, which is where the actual engineering difficulty of these systems lives.

title: RAG or fine-tuning is the wrong first question
text: So when someone asks in week one whether you are doing RAG or fine-tuning, the useful reply is: *show me fifty questions and the answers you want.* The ensuing eleven weeks are not a delay. They are the project.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: # Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The RAG prototype works. Two hundred documents, embeddings in a vector store, and the answers are good enough that somebody says "production".

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: At 10,000 documents it falls apart. Not gradually — the answers become confidently wrong, which is worse than becoming vague.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The engineering fixes for this are real and I will summarise them. But the reason I have titled this issue the way I have is that on the three RAG systems I have worked on, **the binding constraint was never the retrieval algorithm.** It was the corpus, and the corpus is a product decision.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: ## The technical half, briefly

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: Three things break, in order.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: **Chunks lose their context.** The standard 1,000-character sliding window produces chunks like:

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text:
> "...this does not apply where the account has been dormant for more than 90
> days. In those cases the holder must re-verify before any withdrawal..."

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: What is that about? "This" refers to something 1,400 characters earlier, in a different chunk. No product name, no section, no document title. At 200 documents it retrieves anyway, because nothing else mentions dormancy. At 10,000 there are 340 chunks mentioning dormancy across 60 products and this one has nothing to distinguish it.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The fix is to put the context *into* the chunk before embedding it — document title, product, section path, prepended as a header. In my experience this one change is worth more than every other retrieval improvement combined, and it is an afternoon.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: **Top-k is the wrong primitive.** `top_k=5` means "always return five things whether or not any are relevant". At scale, three of the five are superficially similar and wrong, and the model uses them, because it has no way to know they are irrelevant. Retrieve fifty, rerank with a cross-encoder, cut at a relevance floor. **Returning fewer than five is a feature. Returning none and saying so is a feature.**

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: **Nobody notices it broke.** The system produces fluent answers throughout. You need thirty to a hundred real questions with known-correct source documents, run on every change, gating deploys.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: That is the engineering, and it is genuinely most of what people need to hear. My colleagues wrote up the production side of this as [retrieval that survives contact with real users](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/rag-that-survives-contact-with-users), and if you are debugging a system right now that is the more immediately useful read.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: ## The product half, which is the actual problem

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: Here is what happened on all three systems, and it took me until the third to recognise the pattern.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: We built retrieval over "the company's documentation". Quality was mediocre. We improved chunking, added reranking, added hybrid search, built the golden set. Quality got better. Still mediocre.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: Then we looked at what we were retrieving *from*, properly, and found:

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text:
- **Four versions of the same policy**, three superseded, none marked as such.
  Retrieval was correctly finding the most semantically similar one, which was
  from 2021.
- **Documents that contradicted each other**, because two departments had
  written guidance independently and nobody had reconciled them. No retrieval
  system resolves that; it is not a retrieval question.
- **Answers that existed only in people's heads.** About 20% of the questions
  users asked had no answer anywhere in the corpus. Support staff improvised,
  and the improvisations were inconsistent and mostly fine.
- **Documents written for a different reader.** Internal process docs written
  for someone who already knows the product, retrieved to answer a question from
  someone who does not.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: None of that is fixable by better retrieval. It is fixable by deciding what the corpus is, which is a product and editorial decision about what your company asserts to be true.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: ## The forcing function

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: On one of these, the most valuable thing the project produced was not the system. It was the process of asking for fifty real questions with correct answers.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: It took eleven weeks to get them. Not because anyone was slow — because:

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text:
- Support, sales and product disagreed about correct answers to roughly a third.
- Several correct answers depended on the customer's contract, which meant the
  answer was a function, not a string.
- Four had answers the legal team would not approve in writing.
- Six had no answer anywhere in the company.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: By the end, the company had agreed answers to its fifty most common questions, which it had never had. The support team got measurably better *before* the AI system shipped.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: And the architecture had become obvious: retrieval over the newly-written canonical answers; the contract-dependent questions routed to a deterministic lookup because they were not a language problem; the legally-sensitive ones escalated to a human by design.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: We could not have chosen that architecture in week one. The information did not exist.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: ## What this means for how you scope one

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The implication I would draw, and it runs against how these projects are usually planned:

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: **A RAG project is a content project with a retrieval system attached.**

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The engineering is maybe a third of the work. The rest is deciding what your company's canonical answers are, writing the ones that do not exist, retiring the superseded versions, and reconciling the contradictions — and all of that requires authority to decide what is true, which engineering does not have.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: So the two questions I would ask before starting:

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text:
1. **Who can decide what the correct answer is?** If the answer is "it depends
   which department you ask", you have found the project's real first phase.
2. **Is anyone willing to retire documents?** A corpus that only grows will
   degrade indefinitely, because every superseded document competes with its
   replacement. This needs an owner and it is nobody's favourite job.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: If both answers are unsatisfying, the retrieval work will produce a system that faithfully surfaces your organisation's existing confusion. Which is, to be fair, diagnostically useful — but it is not what was in the business case.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: ## The uncomfortable version

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The most useful framing I have for this: **a retrieval system is a mirror.** It will show you, with uncomfortable precision, that your documentation is four years out of date, that two departments disagree, and that a fifth of what your customers ask is answered by institutional memory rather than by anything written down.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: Teams respond to that by tuning the retrieval, because the retrieval is the part they own. It does not help. You cannot rank your way out of a corpus that contains three contradictory answers; whichever one you surface, you are wrong two-thirds of the time, and the better your retrieval the more confidently you are wrong.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: The grounding for all this — what retrieval is actually doing, and why it beats retraining for knowledge that changes — is explained more patiently than I have managed here in [a plain-English explanation of what RAG is doing](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-rag-in-ai), which is a reasonable thing to send a non-technical stakeholder who is about to sponsor one of these.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: My one practical recommendation: before any engineering, spend two weeks getting fifty real questions and their agreed answers. If that takes eleven weeks instead, you have learned the most important thing about the project, and you have learned it for the price of two weeks rather than two quarters.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: Next issue: how to buy engineering capacity, and the four contract clauses that took me two failures to work out.

title: Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
Issue 6: Retrieval is a product problem
text: *I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three RAG systems, anonymised; the eleven-week figure is from one of them and I have rounded nothing about it, because it is the detail I most want people to believe.*

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: # Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: An agent is a loop: model decides, tool runs, result goes back, repeat until done. Forty lines of code. The demo is genuinely impressive and takes an afternoon.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Then you put it in front of real inputs and discover what the loop does when it is confused. It does not stop. It retries the same failing tool eleven times. It calls a paid API in a cycle. It decides that the way to resolve an ambiguous instruction is to try every interpretation. One of ours, early on, spent $340 in nineteen minutes re-reading the same document because a downstream parse error made it believe each read had failed.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: None of that is a model problem. It is a missing control plane. Here is the one I would build on day one now, rather than day forty.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## The loop, unguarded

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: For reference, the thing we are hardening:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: `max_turns` is the only guard, and it is the wrong unit. Twenty turns can mean two cheap calls or two hundred expensive ones, depending on how many tool calls the model batches per turn.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## Budget in the units that actually hurt

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Track three things, because they fail independently:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: `remaining_note` is the non-obvious one and it changes behaviour a lot. An agent that knows it has two turns left will summarise and conclude. An agent that is killed at turn twenty produces nothing. Telling the model its budget converts a hard failure into a degraded success.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: **Per-tool budgets too**, because the aggregate does not catch the pathological case:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text:
```python
@dataclass
class ToolPolicy:
    max_calls: int = 10
    max_identical_calls: int = 2   # the one that saved us $340
    cost_per_call_usd: float = 0.0
    requires_approval: bool = False
```

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: `max_identical_calls` deserves its own paragraph. The single most common agent pathology is calling the same tool with the same arguments repeatedly, because the result did not change the model's situation and so the model's reasoning arrives at the same next step. Hash the call:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text:
```python
def call_signature(name, arguments):
    canonical = json.dumps(arguments, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{name}:{canonical}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
```

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: On the third identical call, do not execute it. Return a synthetic result that tells the model what is happening:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Models respond to this well. It breaks the loop about 80% of the time without aborting the task.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## The kill switch has to work from outside the process

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: A flag checked at the top of the loop is not a kill switch if the loop is running in a worker you cannot reach. You need two levels.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: **Level 1 — cooperative, checked every iteration:**

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: `control` reads from somewhere operationally reachable — Redis, a feature flag service, a database row. The property that matters: an on-call engineer can stop a running agent in under thirty seconds without a deploy and without finding the right pod.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: **Level 2 — a global circuit breaker**, because the thing you most often need to stop is not one agent but all of them:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Spend rate is the one to implement first. It is the failure that gets noticed by finance rather than by monitoring, which is a bad way to find out.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## Classify tools by what they can destroy

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Not all tools need the same treatment. Three tiers:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text:
```python
TOOL_TIERS = {
    # Read-only. Cheap, idempotent, no approval.
    "search_documents":  Tier.READ,
    "get_customer":      Tier.READ,

    # Writes to systems we control and can undo.
    "create_draft":      Tier.REVERSIBLE,
    "update_ticket":     Tier.REVERSIBLE,

    # Outward-facing or irreversible. Never autonomous.
    "send_email":        Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
    "issue_refund":      Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
    "delete_record":     Tier.IRREVERSIBLE,
}
```

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: The rule we settled on: **`IRREVERSIBLE` tools are never called by the agent.** The agent *proposes* them, the proposal goes to a human or to a deterministic rule engine, and the action executes outside the loop.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: This sounds like it defeats the purpose. It does not. In the deployments that have actually worked, the agent's value was in the reasoning and the assembly — reading six systems, working out what the situation is, drafting the response. The final send is one click. Making that click a human's costs almost nothing in throughput and removes the entire category of failure where an agent emails four hundred customers.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: If you do want autonomous irreversible actions, gate them on value:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: A refund under $50 can be autonomous. A refund over $5,000 cannot. That is a business rule, written in code, outside the model.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## Traces, or you are debugging blind

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: Every run emits one trace, with a span per model call and per tool call, and the attributes you need at 2am:

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text:
```python
with tracer.start_span("agent.run") as run_span:
    run_span.set_attributes({
        "agent.run_id": run_id,
        "agent.task_type": task_type,
        "agent.budget.max_cost_usd": budget.max_cost_usd,
    })
    ...
    with tracer.start_span("agent.tool_call") as span:
        span.set_attributes({
            "tool.name": call.name,
            "tool.tier": TOOL_TIERS[call.name].name,
            "tool.signature": sig,
            "tool.repeat_count": seen[sig],
            "tool.duration_ms": duration_ms,
            "tool.is_error": is_error,
        })
```

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: `tool.signature` and `tool.repeat_count` are what let you find loop pathologies in aggregate rather than one anecdote at a time. Query for runs where any signature repeated more than twice and you have a list of your prompt's weaknesses, ranked by frequency.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: The OpenTelemetry project has [semantic conventions for GenAI spans](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) now; using them rather than inventing attribute names means your traces work in whatever tooling you adopt later.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: ## What this adds up to

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: The loop is 40 lines. The control plane around it is maybe 400, and that ratio is the honest shape of agent engineering. Budget in three units, per-tool call limits with identical-call detection, an out-of-process kill switch, a spend-rate circuit breaker, a tool tier model where irreversible actions are proposals, and traces with call signatures.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: None of it is clever. All of it is the difference between a demo and something you can leave running.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: If you are at the start of this, Pixorama's guide on [how to build an AI agent](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-agent) covers the loop and the tool-definition side in more detail than I have here, and their survey of [fifteen ways companies are using them right now](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases) is a useful sanity check on scope — most of the deployments that work are narrower than the ones people plan.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: If you are considering an agency for this rather than building in-house, the control plane above is the thing to interrogate them about. Most agency demos show the loop; very few show a spend-rate circuit breaker or a tool tier model. Pixorama's guide to [choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c) has a section on telling builders from resellers, and "show me your kill switch" is the shortest version of that test I know.

title: Giving an AI agent a tool-call budget and a kill switch
text: The [Model Context Protocol spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) is also worth reading before you design your tool layer, if only because standardising on it means your tool definitions outlive your framework choice.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: # How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: I have been in the room for maybe thirty of these, on both sides. The pitches are remarkably similar, which is itself informative: they have converged on a format that works on buyers, and that format is largely decoupled from whether the agency is any good.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: This is not a post about which agencies to hire. It is about the six questions that produce different answers from good and bad agencies, and why the standard pitch is constructed to avoid them.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## First, what the standard pitch contains

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: You will almost always get, in this order: a site audit with a number of "errors" found, a list of keywords you are not ranking for with their search volumes, a competitor comparison showing you behind, some case studies with percentage increases, and a proposal with a monthly retainer and a list of deliverables.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Every element of that is designed to establish that there is a problem and that they have a process. None of it establishes that their process caused the results in their case studies, which is the only thing you are actually buying.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: So: six questions.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 1. "What was this client's traffic before you started, in absolute numbers?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Case studies are quoted in percentages. Percentages are chosen because they are large.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: "We grew organic traffic 340%" from 200 visits a month to 880 is a real achievement on a tiny site and tells you almost nothing about what they could do for a site with 40,000 visits. The mechanisms that take you from 200 to 880 — fixing indexation, writing the first twenty pages, claiming the brand term — do not exist on a mature site.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Ask for absolute before-and-after, the time period, and the starting domain authority. A good agency gives you all three without flinching. An agency that only has percentages is telling you their wins were on small sites, or that the baseline was unflattering.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Follow-up worth asking: *what happened to that client's traffic in the twelve months after the engagement ended?* The answer separates agencies who build assets from agencies who rent you rankings.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 2. "Which of those results would have happened anyway?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: This is the question that produces the most interesting silence.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Organic traffic grows for lots of reasons: the market grew, a competitor exited, a Google update happened to favour the site's shape, seasonality, a PR event, a product launch, the brand got better known through paid channels.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: A good SEO agency has thought carefully about attribution, because they want credit for the right things. They will talk about non-brand traffic separately from brand, segment by landing page, and reference a baseline or a control.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: An agency that has never considered the counterfactual is either not analytical or is relying on you not asking. Both are disqualifying.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: A specific probe: *do you report brand and non-brand organic separately?* If they do not, their headline number includes people typing the company name, which SEO did not cause.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 3. "What will you do in month one that is not an audit?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Audits are the agency's cheapest deliverable and your least valuable one. A crawler produces an audit in twenty minutes; the consultant writes a summary. Most of the "errors" are low-impact — missing alt text, meta descriptions a few characters too long, a handful of redirect chains.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: That work is not useless, but it is rarely why a site does not rank. It is popular because it is schedulable, demonstrable, and requires no judgement.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: The question tests whether they have a thesis about *your* site. A good answer sounds like: "your category pages are competing with your blog posts for the same terms, and the blog posts are winning, which is why the commercial pages do not convert — we would fix that information architecture first." That is a hypothesis with a mechanism.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: A bad answer is a list of deliverables.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 4. "How many links will you build, from where, and would you show me the last ten?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Authority is usually the binding constraint — in my experience most sites that are stuck are stuck on authority, not on-page work — so this is the most important question and the one with the most evasive answers.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: The honest spectrum:

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text:
- **"We do digital PR; links are earned and we cannot guarantee numbers."** This
  is the credible answer. It is also slow and expensive, and they should say so.
- **"We have relationships with publishers in your sector."** Plausible. Ask to
  see examples and check whether those sites have genuine audiences or exist to
  host paid placements.
- **"We'll build 40 links a month."** Nobody earns 40 editorial links a month.
  These are bought, from a network, and the risk sits with you.
- **"Links are not that important any more."** This is usually said by agencies
  that cannot build them.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Then ask for the last ten links they built for any client. Look at the pages they are on. Does the page have other content? Does the site have real traffic? Is your link one of nine outbound commercial links in a 600-word post about nothing?

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: The reason this matters more than the rest combined: on-page work has a ceiling set by your authority. If your domain has a few dozen referring domains and the page-one incumbents have hundreds, no amount of content optimisation closes that. An agency selling you content when your constraint is authority is selling you the thing they can deliver rather than the thing you need.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 5. "What would make you tell me to stop paying you?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: A real consultant has a view on when their work stops being worth it. Answers I have heard and respected:

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text:
- "If your product pages do not convert, more traffic is a waste — fix that
  first."
- "Your category is dominated by three marketplaces; you will not outrank them,
  and you would do better on the long tail or on a different channel."
- "You have a six-week dev queue. SEO recommendations that cannot be implemented
  are not worth paying for."

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: That last one is the single most common real blocker and almost no agency raises it in a pitch. SEO is largely a series of changes to a website; if your engineering team cannot ship them, the retainer buys you a backlog.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: An agency with no answer to this question has not located the boundary of their own usefulness, which means they will keep invoicing past it.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## 6. "Who, specifically, will do the work?"

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: The person pitching is frequently not the person delivering. Normal, and fine if disclosed.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Ask for the named individual, their experience, how many other accounts they carry, and whether any of it is subcontracted. Then ask to speak to them before signing.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Twelve accounts per strategist means roughly three hours a month on yours. That can be fine for maintenance and is not enough to change anything. The arithmetic is worth doing out loud: divide the retainer by a plausible blended rate and see how many hours you are actually buying. The gap between that number and the promised deliverables is the honest measure of the proposal.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## The pattern underneath all six

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Each question asks the same thing in a different register: **is there a causal story, and can you show me the mechanism?**

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Good SEO is unglamorous and mostly consists of: making the site crawlable and fast, organising information so that one page answers one intent, building genuine authority slowly through work that is hard to fake, and removing whatever is preventing the engineering team from shipping changes. Agencies that do this are usually less impressive in a pitch than agencies that do not, because their story has fewer numbers in it and more caveats.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: The structural problem is that the pitch rewards confidence and the work rewards patience, so the selection process is biased against the thing you want.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: ## A note on how the market looks from the inside

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: One more thing, since it is relevant to anyone reading agency comparison lists.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: Search "best SEO agencies" plus any country and you will find dozens of listicle pages, most of them published by agencies, directories, or content sites with no assessment process. The ordering is frequently commercial. They cite each other.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: That is not a reason to ignore them entirely — they are a reasonable way to assemble a longlist of names you had not heard of. It is a reason not to treat the ordering as a ranking. The useful move is to take the names and apply the six questions, which is work the list has not done for you.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: If you are shortlisting in Australia specifically, a survey of [the Australian agency landscape](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia) is a reasonable place to collect names across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth before you start asking questions. And if what you actually need turns out to be implementation capacity rather than strategy — which question 5 frequently reveals — [Australian web development firms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/top-web-development-companies-australia) may be the more useful shortlist, because an SEO retainer on top of a blocked dev queue is money for recommendations nobody will implement.

title: How to read an SEO agency pitch without getting sold
text: That is, genuinely, the most common outcome I have seen: the company did not need an SEO agency. It needed two engineering sprints and someone with authority to decide what the category pages are for.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: # Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: I said in issue one that this was the topic where I am most likely to be wrong, so let me be specific enough to be wrong usefully.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Four agent builds in the last eighteen months. Three should not have been agents. One genuinely needed to be. All four shipped and all four work, which is why this is a subtle argument rather than a horror story — the three that should not have been agents cost between four and nine times what the alternative would have cost, and two of them are less reliable than a state machine. That is the expensive kind of success, and it is much harder to learn from than failure.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## The test, which takes an afternoon

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Before any discussion of frameworks or models:

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **Can you draw the decision tree?**

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Not "is it complicated". Not "does it have a lot of branches". Just: if you sat down with a domain expert and enough patience, could you enumerate the decision points and what determines each one?

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: If yes, you have a workflow. Write the workflow. You may well want a model *inside* it — for extraction, classification, summarisation, drafting — but the control flow belongs in code, where it is deterministic, testable, cheap and explainable.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: If genuinely no — if the sequence depends on what you discover while doing it, in a way you cannot enumerate in advance — you need something that decides at runtime. That is an agent.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: That is the whole test. An afternoon with a whiteboard, undertaken *hoping to succeed*, would have saved three projects a lot of money.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## The three that failed it

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **An invoice processor.** Brief: "an agent that handles supplier invoices." Actual requirement: extract fields from a PDF, match the purchase order, check against tolerance, route exceptions, post to the ledger. Five steps, fixed order, every branch enumerable.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: The extraction step benefits enormously from a model — 400 suppliers in 400 layouts is exactly what models are good at. The control flow is a flowchart somebody in accounts payable drew in 2019.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: As an agent it was non-deterministic in a domain where auditors require you to explain why a specific invoice went to a specific approver. "The model decided" does not survive a controls review, and we spent six weeks building trace tooling to reconstruct decisions a `switch` statement would have made legible for free.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **An onboarding assistant.** Document collection with conditional requirements by entity type and jurisdiction. Complicated — about ninety rows of decision table. Not unknowable: the compliance team maintained that table in a spreadsheet.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: We built an agent that read the policy documents and reasoned about which documents were required. It was right about 92% of the time. The spreadsheet was right 100% of the time, because it *was* the policy.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: This is the failure mode I find hardest to forgive in myself: using a probabilistic system to approximate a deterministic rule that already existed in written form. We built lossy compression of a lookup table.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **An internal support bot.** The answering half was retrieval and worked well. The taking-actions half was the problem: it occasionally chained actions in ways nobody intended, granting an access request as a step toward resolving an unrelated ticket. Technically helpful; also a security incident.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## The one that passed

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: A diagnostic assistant for field-service engineers. Someone arrives at industrial equipment that is not working, describes symptoms, and the system helps diagnose it.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Five properties made this genuinely agent-shaped:

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text:
1. **The next step depends on what the last step revealed**, and the symptom
   space is combinatorial rather than listable.
2. **The right information source is not known in advance** — manuals, past
   tickets, telemetry, parts inventory, an engineer's free-text note from 2019 —
   and which to consult depends on the hypothesis being tested.
3. **A human is in the loop continuously.** The engineer is standing in front of
   the machine, feeding in observations and rejecting bad suggestions.
4. **Being wrong is cheap.** The engineer says "no, that's not it." Being right
   is valuable.
5. **The decision tree had been attempted and had failed.** Twice, with a rules
   engine. Unmaintainable within a year both times.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: That fifth property is the one I would weight most heavily, and it is the cheapest to check. If nobody has tried to write the rules, the claim that the rules cannot be written is unevidenced.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Those five together are rare. When all five hold, the agent framing is not just acceptable but clearly right.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## Why the costume gets worn

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Three forces, none of them stupidity:

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **The demo is seductive and the hard part is invisible.** An agent that handles one happy path takes an afternoon. The control plane that makes it safe — budgets in cost and turns, loop detection, tool tiering, traces, evaluation harness — is roughly ten times the loop, and none of it shows in the demo.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **"Agent" is how the work gets funded.** A proposal to build a workflow with two model calls competes against a proposal to build an AI agent. The second wins, even when it is the same project described worse.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **The framework encourages it.** If the easiest thing to build is a loop, people build a loop.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## The shape that is usually right

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: For most business problems the answer is not agent-or-workflow. It is a deterministic workflow with model calls at the perception and generation steps:

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text:
```
[intake] → (model: extract) → [validate] → [branch on rules]
                                                  │
                            ┌─────────────────────┴──────────────┐
                      [happy path]                       [exception path]
                            │                                   │
                  (model: draft reply)                   [human review]
                            │                                   │
                        [send]                              [resolve]
```

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Square brackets are code. Parentheses are model calls. The model does perception and language; code makes decisions.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: This is dull and has the properties that matter: every path is testable, every decision is explainable to an auditor, cost per transaction is predictable, failures are attributable to a step, and you can change business rules without re-evaluating a prompt.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: And when an agent genuinely is needed, **put it inside one step of this workflow** rather than around the whole thing. The diagnostic assistant is an agent living inside a service-ticket workflow: the ticket lifecycle is deterministic, the diagnosis step is agentic. That containment is what makes it operable.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## The rule I would not bend

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: For anything irreversible or outward-facing — sending an email, issuing a refund, granting access, deleting a record — **the agent proposes and code or a human decides.** Always.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: This sounds like it defeats the purpose and it does not. In every deployment I have seen work, the value was in the reasoning and the assembly: reading six systems, working out what the situation is, drafting the response. The final send is one click. Making that click a human's costs almost nothing in throughput and eliminates the entire category of failure where an agent emails four hundred customers.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: If you want autonomy on irreversible actions, gate it on value — a refund under $50 can be autonomous, one over $5,000 cannot. That is a business rule, in code, outside the model.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: ## Where I might be wrong

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Two places, stated so they can be checked later.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **The test may be too conservative.** "Can you draw the decision tree" catches cases where drawing it is *possible but uneconomic* — a tree with 4,000 branches that would take a year to enumerate and a year to maintain. The onboarding case had ninety rows, which is clearly worth writing. At what size does that flip? I do not know, and I suspect the honest answer is that it depends on how fast the rules change rather than on their count.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: **Model capability may move the line.** My objections to the three failures are largely about determinism and explainability, which are properties of the architecture rather than the model's intelligence. Those objections should be stable. But the reliability objection — 92% versus 100% — is a capability claim, and capability claims age badly. If that gap closes, the onboarding case gets closer to reasonable, though I would still want to know why you would prefer an inferred policy to a written one.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: For a wider view than my four, my colleagues catalogued [fifteen use cases they have catalogued](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases) across different industries, and what strikes me reading it is how much narrower the successful deployments are than the way these projects get pitched internally. The narrowest and most reliable category is the one that barely looks like an agent at all — [the receptionist-versus-answering-service comparison](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-answering-service-vs-human-receptionist) is a good example of a bounded task with a clear fallback, which is why it works.

title: Issue 5: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where they don't
text: Next issue: retrieval, and why the demo-to-production gap is almost entirely chunking.
