title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: # Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Here is the conversation that happens about four weeks after an agent ships.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
> "Is it working?"
> "Users seem happy."
> "Should we change the prompt to handle the refund case better?"
> "Probably?"
> "Will that break anything else?"
> "...we'd find out."

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: That is not an engineering practice. And the reason teams end up there is that agent evaluation looks like a research problem — benchmarks, LLM-as-judge, accuracy percentages — when the production version is mostly a boring observability problem with three artefacts.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## Why "accuracy" is the wrong top-line metric

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: An agent that answers 94% of questions correctly sounds good. It depends entirely on the 6%.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Six percent wrong answers delivered confidently, in a customer-facing context, is a worse product than 70% correct answers and 30% "I'll get a human." The distribution of failure matters more than the rate, and a single accuracy number deliberately hides it.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: So the metrics that are worth putting on a dashboard:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
| Metric | What it tells you | Target direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Task completion rate** | Did it finish without escalating? | Up, but not at the expense of the next row |
| **Confident-wrong rate** | Finished, answer was wrong | **Down, hard. This is the one that matters.** |
| **Appropriate escalation rate** | Didn't know, said so | Up — this is a success, not a failure |
| **Loop rate** | Repeated the same call ≥3× | Down; it is a prompt defect |
| **Cost per completed task** | Unit economics | Down, watch for it trading against quality |
| **p95 latency to resolution** | Usability | Down |

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: The second row is the expensive one to measure, because it needs ground truth. The others come free from traces.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## Artefact 1: traces that answer questions at 2am

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Every run emits one trace. Spans for the run, each model call, each tool call. This is table stakes and most teams have some version of it; the attributes are what make it useful.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```python
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("agent")

def run_agent(task, tools, budget, ctx):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("agent.run") as run:
        run.set_attributes({
            "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
            "gen_ai.system": "anthropic",
            "agent.run_id": ctx.run_id,
            "agent.task_type": classify_task(task),   # <- critical
            "agent.tenant_id": ctx.tenant_id,
            "agent.entry_point": ctx.entry_point,
        })
        try:
            outcome = _loop(task, tools, budget, ctx)
            run.set_attributes({
                "agent.outcome": outcome.kind,          # completed|escalated|aborted
                "agent.turns": budget.turns,
                "agent.tool_calls": budget.tool_calls,
                "agent.cost_usd": budget.cost_usd,
                "agent.max_repeat_count": outcome.max_repeat,
            })
            return outcome
        except BudgetExceeded as e:
            run.set_attributes({"agent.outcome": "aborted", "agent.abort_reason": e.limit})
            raise
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: `agent.task_type` is the attribute that converts traces from anecdotes into analysis. Without it, your dashboard says "87% completion" across a population of wildly different tasks. With it, you discover completion is 97% for `order_status` and 41% for `billing_dispute`, which is an actionable finding and also the thing you would have found eventually by reading complaints.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Classify cheaply and deterministically — a keyword rule or a small classifier. Do not use the agent itself to classify its own task type; you need this attribute to be reliable when the agent is misbehaving.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: The [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) define standard names for the model-call attributes (`gen_ai.*`). Use them for anything they cover so your traces are portable across tooling, and namespace your own under `agent.*`.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## Artefact 2: the golden set, built from production

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Thirty to a hundred real tasks with known-correct outcomes. Not invented tasks — invented ones are systematically easier, because you write them in the vocabulary your system already handles.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Harvest from traces:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```python
def harvest_candidates(window_days=14, per_type=12):
    """Pull a stratified sample for human labelling. Deliberately
    oversamples failures, because that is where the information is."""
    buckets = {}
    for run in traces.query(window_days=window_days):
        key = (run["agent.task_type"], run["agent.outcome"])
        buckets.setdefault(key, []).append(run)

    sample = []
    for (task_type, outcome), runs in buckets.items():
        # 2:1 weighting toward non-completed outcomes
        n = per_type if outcome == "completed" else per_type * 2
        sample.extend(random.sample(runs, min(n, len(runs))))
    return sample
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Then a human labels each: what *should* have happened. This is a day of someone's time and there is no substitute for it. LLM-as-judge is useful for scaling a rubric you have already validated against human labels; it is not useful for establishing the rubric, because its failure modes correlate with the agent's.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Store each case with the full input context, not just the question:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```python
@dataclass
class GoldenCase:
    id: str
    task_type: str
    input: dict                  # full context, incl. tenant state at the time
    expected_outcome: str        # completed | escalated
    expected_assertions: list    # see below
    notes: str                   # why a human judged it this way
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: **Assertions, not expected strings.** An agent's output is non-deterministic prose; string-matching it produces a test suite that fails on paraphrase. Assert on properties:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```python
expected_assertions = [
    Contains("refund"),                      # mentions the right concept
    MentionsAmount(142.50),                  # gets the number right
    NotContains("account number"),           # no PII leakage
    CalledTool("get_order"),                 # did the necessary lookup
    DidNotCallTool("issue_refund"),          # did NOT act autonomously
    ToolCallCountAtMost(6),                  # didn't flail
    Escalated(),                             # handed off appropriately
]
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: `CalledTool` / `DidNotCallTool` assertions are where most of the real value is. Behavioural assertions on the trajectory are far more stable than assertions on the final text, and they catch the failures you actually care about — an agent that reaches the right answer by calling `issue_refund` twice is not a success.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## Artefact 3: the regression gate

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Run the golden set on every prompt change, tool change, and model version change. Block the deploy on regression.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: The gate has three conditions, and the second is the one teams forget:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```python
def gate(current, baseline):
    failures = []

    # 1. No hard-assertion failures, ever. PII leakage, autonomous
    #    irreversible actions, wrong monetary amounts.
    if current.hard_failures > 0:
        failures.append(f"{current.hard_failures} hard assertion failures")

    # 2. No per-task-type regression, even if the aggregate improved.
    #    This is the one that catches "fixed refunds, broke returns".
    for task_type, score in current.by_task_type.items():
        prior = baseline.by_task_type.get(task_type)
        if prior and score < prior - 0.05:
            failures.append(f"{task_type} regressed {prior:.2f} -> {score:.2f}")

    # 3. Cost did not balloon for equivalent quality.
    if current.mean_cost > baseline.mean_cost * 1.3:
        failures.append(f"cost +{(current.mean_cost/baseline.mean_cost - 1):.0%}")

    return failures
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Condition 2 exists because prompt engineering is a zero-sum game more often than anyone admits. You add an instruction to handle billing disputes better, the model reweights, and order-status handling quietly degrades. The aggregate score goes up. The per-type breakdown shows what you actually did.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: I would go further: **treat the prompt as code under review**, with the eval diff attached to the pull request:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
```
$ make eval
  baseline: prompt@a3f9c21   current: prompt@HEAD
  
  task_type          baseline  current   delta
  order_status          0.97     0.91    -0.06  REGRESSION
  billing_dispute       0.41     0.78    +0.37
  refund_request        0.88     0.89    +0.01
  address_change        0.94     0.94     0.00
  ---
  aggregate             0.80     0.88    +0.08
  mean cost/task       $0.031   $0.047   +52%   WARN
  hard failures            0        0
  
  GATE: FAILED (order_status regression; cost +52%)
```

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: That output makes the trade-off explicit and arguable. "Aggregate +8%" would have shipped it.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## Online: shadow mode, then ramp

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Offline evals tell you about the distribution you sampled. Production has a different one.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: **Shadow mode** before anything user-facing: run the new version alongside the current one, serve the current answer, record both, diff them. The disagreement rate is your risk estimate, and inspecting fifty disagreements is the fastest way to find out whether the new version is better or differently-wrong.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: **Then ramp by task type, not by percentage.** 5% of all traffic exposes every task type to the new version. 100% of `order_status` and 0% of everything else limits the blast radius to the category you have the most evidence about, and it is much easier to interpret.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: Keep the kill switch reachable without a deploy. You will use it.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: ## The minimum viable version

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: If this is more than you can build this quarter, the order of return:

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text:
1. **Traces with `task_type` and `outcome`.** A day's work. Converts "users seem
   happy" into a number per category.
2. **Thirty golden cases with behavioural assertions.** Another day, mostly
   labelling. This is what makes change safe.
3. **The per-task-type regression gate.** An afternoon, once you have 1 and 2.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: That is three days for a practice that holds up for years. Steps 1 and 2 in either order; step 3 is worthless without both.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: For a grounded view of which agent deployments are actually in production and earning their keep — which is a useful corrective if your roadmap has eleven agent initiatives on it — Pixorama's survey of [where agents are actually being deployed](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/ai-agents-for-business-use-cases) is a reasonable reality check. And if you are evaluating a vendor platform rather than building, their buyer's guide on what [survives real production traffic](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/conversational-ai-platform-buyers-guide) asks most of the right questions, particularly about whether you can export your own traces — which, if you cannot, means you cannot build any of this.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: The same test applies to agencies. Pixorama's guide to [choosing an AI automation agency](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-ai-automation-agencies-in-the-usa-and-australia-for-2026-how-to-c) separates firms that build from firms that resell, and the cleanest version of that question is this post's subject: ask what they measure, and whether you get the traces. An agency that cannot show you a per-task-type breakdown of their last deployment is describing a demo.

title: Evaluating an AI agent in production: traces, golden sets and regression gates
text: The one-line version: instrument `task_type`, label thirty real cases, gate on per-type regression. Everything else in agent evaluation is refinement on top of those three.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: # Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: We tried staff augmentation twice and got burned twice. The third time it worked well enough that two of those engineers are still on the team four years later, as employees.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: Nothing changed about the model, the vendor quality, or our engineering practice between attempt two and attempt three. What changed was four clauses in the contract, and in retrospect both earlier failures were entirely predictable from the documents we signed.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: I am writing this because the standard post-mortem for a failed augmentation engagement is "the contractors weren't good enough", and in both of our cases that was false and also convenient.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: ## Failure one: we bought headcount instead of capability

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: The brief was "four backend engineers for six months." We got four backend engineers. They were, on paper and in interview, fine.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: What went wrong: we had a system with fourteen years of accumulated context, and we had assumed that "backend engineer" was a fungible unit. The first eight weeks were spent on onboarding, during which our two most senior people were unavailable for anything else because they were answering questions.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: So for two months we had *negative* capacity. Six engineers' worth of salary producing less output than the two we started with. The engagement was six months, which meant we got four months of productive work from four people, minus two months of our seniors' time — call it a net gain of two or three person-months for six person-months of cost.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: Then the engagement ended and the context left with them.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: **What I got wrong:** I was solving for a headcount gap when the actual constraint was context. Adding people to a context-heavy system does not add capacity in the short term; it subtracts it. This is the thing Brooks wrote down fifty years ago and I had read and had not internalised.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: ## Failure two: nobody owned the output

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: Second attempt, smarter brief: two engineers, twelve months, one specific subsystem.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: Better. And it failed differently.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: The vendor's engineers reported to a vendor delivery manager. Our team lead gave them work. When priorities conflicted — and they did, constantly, because the vendor was tracking against a statement of work and we were tracking against a sprint — the engineers were put in an impossible position and resolved it by following whoever asked most recently.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: The subsystem got built. It worked. It also did not match how the rest of our system was built, because the code review that would have caught that never happened consistently — our engineers reviewed the vendor's PRs when they had time, and when they did not, the vendor's own delivery manager approved them to keep the SOW on schedule.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: We spent four months after the engagement ended reworking it. That rework was not in anyone's cost model.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: **What I got wrong:** I treated the engagement as a delivery contract when I needed it to be a capacity contract. A delivery contract makes the vendor accountable for an outcome, which sounds good and means they control the process. For work inside your own codebase, you want to control the process.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: ## The four clauses

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: Third attempt. Same model, same category of vendor. These four things were in the contract.

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text: ### 1. Our definition of done, in the contract, by reference

title: Staff augmentation failed us twice before we wrote the contract properly
text:
> "Work is complete when it satisfies the Client's engineering standards as
> published at [internal URL], including code review approval by a Client
> engineer, test coverage thresholds, and documentation requirements. The

text: # Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Most "zero-trust programme" slide decks never reach production. Meanwhile the single change with the best ratio of risk reduction to effort sits untouched in every CI system: a static cloud access key, in a secret store, with broad permissions and no expiry, usable by anyone who can trigger a workflow.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: That key is the most valuable credential in most organisations. It outranks individual engineer access because it is scoped to deploy, which means it can modify production. And it is long-lived, so a single leak — a logged environment variable, a compromised dependency, a fork PR with a misconfigured trigger — is a persistent compromise rather than a time-boxed one.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: OIDC federation removes it entirely. No key anywhere, credentials that live fifteen minutes, and a trust policy that can be scoped to one repository on one branch. This is a day's work and it is worth more than a quarter of policy documents.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## What is actually happening

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: The CI provider becomes an identity provider. Instead of presenting a secret, your workflow presents a signed JWT describing itself — this repo, this branch, this workflow, this event type. Your cloud account verifies the signature against the provider's public keys and, if the claims match a trust policy you wrote, hands back temporary credentials.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text:
```
[workflow] --(1) request JWT--> [CI provider OIDC endpoint]
[workflow] <-(2) signed JWT----
[workflow] --(3) AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity + JWT--> [STS]
                                                      |
                                      (4) verify sig against provider JWKS
                                      (5) match claims against trust policy
[workflow] <-(6) 15-minute credentials ---------------
```

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Nothing is stored. There is no secret to leak, rotate, or inherit when someone leaves.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## The trust policy is the whole security control

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: This is where the mistakes happen, so it is worth being slow here.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Three things about that `sub` claim:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: **It is `StringEquals`, not `StringLike`.** The common catastrophic misconfiguration is:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: which trusts every repository in the org, including the one a contractor has write access to. Worse, I have seen:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: which trusts **every GitHub repository on the internet** to assume your production deploy role. That is not a hypothetical; it has been found in real accounts, because it is what you get when someone debugs a claims mismatch by loosening the condition until it works.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: **It pins the branch.** `ref:refs/heads/main` means a workflow on a feature branch cannot assume this role. If you need deploys from tags, add a second condition value for `ref:refs/tags/*` — explicitly, with `StringLike` scoped to the tag namespace only.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: **Pull requests need separate treatment.** The `pull_request` event produces `sub` of `repo:acme/payments-service:pull_request`, which notably does **not** identify the source branch. A PR from a fork can therefore satisfy a `pull_request`-scoped trust policy. So: PR workflows get a read-only role, never the deploy role. Non-negotiable.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Pin the environment instead when you want approval gates:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text:
```json
"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
  "repo:acme/payments-service:environment:production"
```

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Combined with a protected environment that requires a reviewer, this means the credential cannot be minted at all until a human approves — the control is in identity, not in a pipeline step someone can reorder.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## The Terraform

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Two details I would insist on:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: **`max_session_duration = 900`.** The default is an hour. A deploy takes minutes. Shortening the window costs nothing and bounds the damage from a credential captured mid-run.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: **A permissions boundary.** The deploy role's own policy says what it can do; the boundary says what it can *never* do, regardless of future policy edits. This is how you stop a well-meaning change from granting the CI role `iam:*`:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: `iam:CreateAccessKey` in that deny list is the important one. It is the privilege-escalation path that converts a 15-minute federated credential back into a permanent key — exactly the thing you just removed.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## The workflow

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text:
```yaml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write      # required to request the JWT
  contents: read       # and nothing else

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production     # gates credential minting on approval
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-deploy-payments-service
          aws-region: ap-southeast-2
          role-duration-seconds: 900

      - run: ./deploy.sh
```

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: `permissions:` declared explicitly at the top is worth calling out. Without it you inherit the repository default, which is frequently write-all. The `id-token: write` permission is what allows the JWT request; everything else should be the minimum the job needs.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## Migrating without a delivery freeze

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: The reason this does not get done is fear of breaking deploys. It does not have to:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text:
1. **Create the OIDC provider and roles alongside the existing keys.** Nothing
   changes yet.
2. **Switch one low-risk service's workflow** to the role. Keep its key in place
   as a rollback.
3. **Watch CloudTrail for both principals.** You want to see the role being used
   and the key going quiet.
4. **Deactivate the key — do not delete it.** Deactivation is instantly
   reversible; deletion is not. Leave it deactivated for a sprint.
5. **Repeat per service**, then delete the deactivated keys.
6. **Add the preventive control** so the problem cannot return:

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Applied at the organisation level, that makes "add a CI access key" something nobody can quietly do at 6pm under deadline. Which is the actual mechanism by which these keys appear.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: Step 3 is the one people skip and then regret. Watching both principals for a few days is how you catch the scheduled job, in a workflow nobody remembered, that still uses the key.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: ## Where this sits in a security programme

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: The argument I would make to anyone running a zero-trust initiative: this is the work. Not the strategy document. An identity-based, short-lived, narrowly-scoped, auditable credential replacing a permanent shared secret in the highest-privilege system you own — in a day, with no delivery freeze.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: That framing matters because security programmes typically fail by stopping delivery, which is the argument in Pixorama's [zero-trust without bringing delivery to a halt](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/zero-trust-without-stopping-delivery). OIDC federation is the clearest example of the pattern: the secure version is also the more convenient one, so it does not need enforcement.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: If you are standing up a new cloud estate, make this part of the [landing zone guardrails](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) from day one rather than retrofitting. Setting the `iam:CreateAccessKey` deny before the first workload lands means you never accumulate the keys in the first place.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: GitHub's [security hardening guide for OpenID Connect](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect) documents the full claim set, including `job_workflow_ref`, which is worth using if you want to pin trust to a specific reusable workflow rather than a branch.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: GitLab, Bitbucket, CircleCI and Buildkite all support the same flow. The claim names differ; the trust-policy reasoning is identical, as is the `StringEquals`-not-`StringLike` rule.

title: Zero-trust in CI: killing long-lived cloud credentials with OIDC
text: If this is work you would outsource, it is a good interview question in both directions — ask a prospective [DevOps consulting firm](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-devops-consulting-companies-india) how they handle CI credentials today. A firm still shipping static access keys into client pipelines in 2026 has told you where their practice sits.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: # The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: I have watched four fractional CTO arrangements. Two worked extremely well. Two were expensive and ended awkwardly, and in both of those cases everyone involved was competent and acting in good faith.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: The difference was not the person. It was whether the company had decided, before the engagement started, what the fractional CTO was allowed to decide — and specifically whether they owned the technical roadmap or advised on it.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: That sounds like a semantic distinction. It is the whole thing.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ## The two failure modes

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ### The advisor with accountability

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: A company hires a fractional CTO two days a week. The brief is strategic guidance: architecture, hiring, vendor selection, technical risk.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: They are, implicitly, accountable for technical outcomes. They are also not present when most decisions get made, because decisions happen in the three days a week they are not there.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: So they arrive on Tuesday to find that a choice has been made — a vendor selected, a schema designed, a library adopted — and their options are to accept it or to relitigate it. Accepting it repeatedly means they are not doing the job. Relitigating it repeatedly makes them an obstacle, and the team learns to route around them.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: I watched this one end with the fractional CTO described as "not commercial enough" and the engineering lead described as "not strategic enough", when the actual problem was that two people had the same job and neither had been told.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ### The decision-maker without context

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: The mirror image. A company gives the fractional CTO real authority — they own technical decisions.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: They make good decisions, judged on their merits. They also make them with one-fifth of the context of a full-time person: they do not know that the customer who drove the last architecture change is about to churn, that the senior engineer is interviewing elsewhere, that the sales team has promised a feature in a demo, or that the "temporary" integration is load-bearing for the largest account.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: Good decisions made on incomplete context look like bad decisions in retrospect, and the person who made them is not there to adjust when the context surfaces.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ## What the two successful ones had in common

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: Both drew an explicit line, in writing, before starting. Not a job description — a decision-rights document. It looked roughly like this:

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Fractional CTO decides:** - Architecture at the system-boundary level: what services exist, what owns what   data, what the integration contracts are - Build-versus-buy for anything over a threshold - Technical hiring bar and the interview process - Vendor selection for infrastructure and platform - Security and compliance posture

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Engineering lead decides:** - Everything inside a service boundary - Sprint content and sequencing - Libraries, patterns, tooling within the agreed architecture - Day-to-day prioritisation and trade-offs

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Jointly, with the CEO breaking ties:** - Roadmap sequencing against commercial commitments - Anything that changes the hiring plan or the budget

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: The specific genius of that split, which I did not appreciate until I saw it work, is that **it assigns decisions by how long they take to reverse, not by how important they are.** The fractional CTO owns the decisions that are expensive to undo and therefore benefit from experience and deliberation. The full-time lead owns the decisions that need context and speed and are cheap to revisit.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: That maps naturally onto the actual constraint: the fractional person has judgement but not presence. Give them the decisions where judgement dominates and presence does not matter much. Two days a week is plenty of time to decide what services exist. It is not enough to decide what the team does on Thursday.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ## The diagnostic

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: If you are considering this, the question is not "should we hire a fractional CTO". It is: **which of these three problems do you have?**

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Problem 1: nobody on the team has made these decisions before.** You have capable engineers who have never designed a multi-tenant system, chosen between managed services at scale, or built a security posture that passes enterprise procurement. They will make these decisions anyway, by default, and some will be expensive.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: *This is the fractional CTO case.* Judgement is the scarce resource and it is needed episodically. Two days a week is genuinely sufficient.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Problem 2: you do not have enough engineers.** The decisions are fine; the throughput is not.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: *This is not the fractional CTO case*, and it is the most common mis-diagnosis. A fractional CTO will not write your features, and hiring one when the constraint is capacity produces a well-architected system that ships slowly. What you want is [augmenting the team you have](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-staff-augmentation) or permanent hires, depending on whether the need is bounded.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Problem 3: nobody is accountable for technical outcomes.** There is no engineering leadership at all. Decisions are made by whoever cares most, which is sometimes a product manager and sometimes the loudest engineer.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: *This is also not the fractional CTO case*, or rather, it is a case where a fractional CTO will fail. You cannot part-time your way into being the person who holds a function together. A fractional person can provide judgement to an existing structure; they cannot be the structure. Hire a full-time engineering lead, even a less experienced one, and give them a fractional CTO to learn from.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: That third configuration — a full-time lead with less experience plus a fractional CTO with more — is, in my observation, the arrangement with the best results and it is rarely what people set out to buy. It is cheaper than a full-time experienced CTO, it develops someone internally, and it covers both presence and judgement.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ## The practical conditions

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: For the engagement to work, four things that are easy to get wrong:

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Fixed days, not flexible hours.** "Two days a week, whenever" means the fractional CTO is never reliably available, so the team stops waiting for them. Fixed days mean decisions can be scheduled.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **Attendance at the meeting where the roadmap is set.** Not a written update afterwards. If they are not in that room, they are advising on a plan rather than shaping it, and the first failure mode above is already in progress.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **A direct line to the CEO or founder.** The value of an experienced technologist is largely in saying "that commercial commitment is not achievable" to the person who made it. Routed through a layer, that message gets softened into uselessness.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: **An explicit end state.** Either the arrangement converts to full-time, or it tapers as the internal lead grows into the role, or it ends at a milestone. An open-ended fractional CTO engagement at month thirty is a sign that the company has outsourced a permanent function, which costs more and builds nothing internally.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: On rates and the commercial shape — day rates, retainer versus equity, what the market actually pays in the US versus Australia — Pixorama has [rates in the US and Australia and when the role makes sense](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-cto) written up with the numbers, which is useful because the published rates vary enormously and the variance is mostly about scope rather than seniority.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: ## The uncomfortable bit

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: The reason this gets decided badly is that the decision-rights conversation is awkward in a way that the hiring conversation is not.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: Telling an incoming experienced technologist "you do not own sprint prioritisation" feels like diminishing the role. Telling your existing engineering lead "you do not own architecture any more" feels like a demotion. Both conversations are easier to avoid, and avoiding them produces the two-people-one-job failure.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: Have them anyway, in week zero, with both people in the room. The version of that conversation held in month seven, after an argument about a vendor choice, is considerably worse.

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: The single question I would make anyone answer before signing: *when the fractional CTO and the engineering lead disagree about an architecture decision, who decides, and does everyone involved already know the answer?*

title: The fractional CTO question is really about who owns the roadmap
text: If the answer is "we'd work it out", the engagement has a predictable ending.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: # Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: I have watched three zero-trust programmes. Two produced documents. One produced change.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: The difference was not budget or executive support — the document-producing ones had more of both. It was that the successful one started with changes where **the secure version was also the more convenient version**, and therefore needed no enforcement.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: That is the whole thesis of this issue, and I want to make it concrete rather than leave it as a slogan.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## Why security programmes stall

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: The standard shape: a maturity assessment, a target-state architecture, a roadmap with workstreams, and a set of controls to be implemented across the estate.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Every control in that roadmap makes someone's job harder. That is not a criticism — it is the nature of a control. But it means every control has a negotiation attached, and the negotiation is between a security team with authority-on-paper and delivery teams with deadlines-in-practice.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Delivery wins those negotiations, mostly, and it wins them by attrition rather than by argument. The control is agreed, scheduled, deprioritised, and raised again next quarter. Two years later the maturity assessment is repeated and the scores have barely moved.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: The programmes that work invert the selection criterion. Instead of asking *what is the highest-risk gap*, they ask **what is the highest-risk gap whose fix makes life easier?** Those exist, there are more of them than people think, and they build the credibility that the genuinely inconvenient controls later require.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## The one I would do this quarter

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Here is the specific example, and I think it is close to universal.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Somewhere in your CI system there is a static cloud access key. It has broad permissions, because deploys need broad permissions. It does not expire. It is usable by anyone who can trigger a workflow or read the secret store.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: That key is plausibly the most valuable credential your organisation holds. It outranks any individual engineer's access, because it is scoped to deploy — which means it can modify production. And because it is long-lived, a single exposure is a persistent compromise rather than a time-boxed one.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Every CI provider now supports OIDC federation, which removes it entirely. The workflow presents a signed token describing itself — this repository, this branch, this environment — your cloud account verifies it against the provider's public keys, and if the claims match a policy you wrote, hands back credentials that live fifteen minutes.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: No key. Nothing to rotate. Nothing to inherit when someone leaves. Nothing to leak.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **And it is less work than the thing it replaces.** No rotation schedule, no secret to manage, no annual audit finding about key age, no "who has access to this secret" question. The engineer whose life you were about to complicate instead has one fewer thing to maintain.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: That asymmetry is why this one actually ships. Nobody has to be persuaded, because there is no trade-off to argue about.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## The two things to get right

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: I will keep this brief because the mechanics are well documented, but these two mistakes are common enough to name.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **Scope the trust policy exactly.** The policy says which identities may assume the role. The failure is loosening it until it works:

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text:
```
"sub": "repo:acme/payments:ref:refs/heads/main"   ← correct
"sub": "repo:acme/*"                               ← trusts every repo in the org
"sub": "*"                                         ← trusts every repo on GitHub
```

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: That third one is not hypothetical. It is what you get when someone debugs a claims mismatch at 6pm by widening the condition until the error stops. Use exact matching, not pattern matching, and review these policies specifically.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **Pull-request workflows get a read-only role.** The token for a pull-request event does not identify the source branch, which means a PR from a fork can satisfy a PR-scoped trust policy. Deploy roles are gated on the protected environment, never on the PR event.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: If you want the full mechanics — trust policy construction, permissions boundaries, and migrating without a delivery freeze — my colleagues have the argument and the implementation in [zero-trust without bringing delivery to a halt](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/zero-trust-without-stopping-delivery).

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## Migrating without a freeze

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: The reason this does not get done, despite being easy, is fear of breaking deploys. It does not require a freeze:

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text:
1. Create the provider and roles **alongside** the existing keys. Nothing
   changes.
2. Switch one low-risk service. Keep its key in place as rollback.
3. **Watch the audit log for both principals** for a few days. This is the step
   people skip and regret — it is how you find the scheduled job in a workflow
   nobody remembered that still uses the key.
4. **Deactivate the key, do not delete it.** Deactivation is instantly
   reversible. Leave it deactivated for a sprint.
5. Repeat per service, then delete.
6. Add an organisation-level policy denying access-key creation, so the problem
   cannot return.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Step six is the one that makes it permanent. Without it, a key reappears within a year, created in a hurry by someone solving a Friday problem — which is how the original one got there.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## The general pattern

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: What makes the CI credential example work, generalised:

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **The control removes a maintenance burden rather than adding one.** Short-lived credentials remove rotation. A managed secret store removes the config file nobody wants to own. Automated patching removes the quarterly scramble.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **The control is preventive rather than detective.** A policy that stops an unencrypted bucket being created is better than an alert that one was created, and it is also less work for everyone — no triage, no remediation ticket, no exception register. Detective controls generate work indefinitely; preventive ones generate work once.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: **The control is enforced by infrastructure rather than by review.** Anything that depends on someone remembering during code review will be missed under deadline, and then the security team's role becomes catching omissions, which is adversarial and does not scale.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: If you order your roadmap by that pattern first, the inconvenient controls afterwards land in a relationship where delivery teams have experienced security work as something that helped them. That is worth more than any amount of executive mandate.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: ## The best time to do this

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Before the estate exists.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Everything above is a retrofit, and retrofits are where security programmes spend their effort. If you are standing up a new cloud environment, the organisation-level deny on access-key creation costs nothing on day one and means you never accumulate the keys at all.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Same for encryption defaults, region allowlists, mandatory tags, and central logging the workload account cannot delete. All trivial before the first workload, all a programme afterwards.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: This is the part that connects to issue two: the landing zone is not preparation for a migration, it is the migration's only durable output. The workloads were going to end up in the cloud anyway. Whether they end up somewhere governable is decided in the weeks before the first one moves, and that is why these controls belong [built into the landing zone before the first workload lands](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/cloud-migration-strategy-on-premise-to-cloud) rather than added later.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: I realise "do it at the start" is useless advice if you are not at the start. So, for the much more common case: pick the one control whose fix removes work, ship it, and use the credibility.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: Next issue, the last one: how to run a vendor shortlist, which is the thing I get asked about most and have the least systematic view of.

title: Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
Issue 9: Security that doesn't stop delivery
text: *I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three programmes, anonymised. I am not a security specialist; this is the view from delivery, which is a partial view and I would be glad to be corrected by someone whose job it actually is.*

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: # One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: The Flutter versus React Native question gets argued on rendering architecture, startup time, and which one "feels native". I have now made this decision four times and in none of them did any of that matter.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: What mattered, every time, was some combination of: what the team already knows, what native capability the app needs, what the existing web codebase looks like, and how much CI complexity the organisation can absorb. Those are build-system and org-chart questions, not framework questions.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Here is the decision procedure I would actually use, and the parts of it that are genuinely technical.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## The framework comparison, dispatched quickly

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Both are mature. Both ship apps used by millions of people. The real architectural difference is one thing:

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: **Flutter draws its own widgets.** It ships a rendering engine and paints to a canvas. You get pixel-identical output across platforms and complete control, and you do not get platform widgets — so when iOS changes its date picker, your app does not.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: **React Native drives platform components.** A `<Text>` becomes a `UITextView` or a `TextView`. You inherit platform behaviour and platform updates for free, and you inherit platform inconsistency.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Everything else — performance, tooling quality, hot reload, ecosystem size — is close enough in 2026 that it should not decide anything. Both have good profilers. Both have adequate state management stories. Both have a long tail of packages of variable quality.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: If your app is a brand-controlled experience with custom design (fintech dashboards, media apps, anything with a strong design system), Flutter's own-rendering model is an advantage. If your app should feel like an OS app and follow platform conventions (utilities, productivity, anything with heavy system integration), React Native's platform-component model is an advantage.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: That is the whole framework analysis. Now the parts that actually decide it.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## Decision input 1: your native-module exposure

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Count the platform capabilities your app needs that are not covered by first-party framework APIs. Bluetooth LE with a specific peripheral profile. Background location with geofencing. A payment terminal SDK. HealthKit. A hardware barcode scanner. CarPlay. An enterprise MDM integration.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: For each one, answer: **is there a maintained community package, and if not, who on the team writes the bridge?**

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
```
Capability             | Flutter pkg      | RN pkg          | Bridge needed?
-----------------------|------------------|-----------------|----------------
BLE (generic)          | mature           | mature          | no
BLE (vendor profile)   | —                | —               | YES, both
Background geofencing  | adequate         | adequate        | no
Payment terminal SDK   | —                | —               | YES, both
HealthKit / Health Conn| adequate         | mature          | no
CarPlay / Android Auto | minimal          | minimal         | YES, both
```

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: If that column has two or more `YES` rows, **the cross-platform framework choice is no longer the main cost of your project.** You are writing native code for both platforms either way, plus the bridge layer, plus the plugin's build integration into your CI. At that point:

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
- Writing bridges in Kotlin/Swift for React Native uses skills that overlap with
  web-native hiring (TypeScript on one side).
- Writing bridges for Flutter needs Dart plus Kotlin plus Swift — three
  languages, and Dart has a smaller hiring pool.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: This is usually the deciding input, and it is almost never in the comparison articles.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## Decision input 2: what your web codebase is

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: If you have a substantial React web app, React Native lets you share genuinely useful things: validation schemas, API clients, domain types, state logic, and business rules. Not components — the sharing-UI-components dream mostly does not work — but the layer underneath, which is frequently 30-40% of the code.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
```
packages/
├── core/              # shared: types, validation, domain logic
│   ├── src/api/       #   generated client from OpenAPI — shared
│   ├── src/domain/    #   pricing rules, entitlements — shared
│   └── src/schema/    #   zod schemas — shared
├── web/               # React
└── mobile/            # React Native — imports @acme/core
```

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: That structure pays for itself in correctness, not just effort: a pricing rule that exists once cannot diverge between platforms. We shipped a bug once where web and mobile disagreed about whether a discount applied to shipping, and it took three weeks to find because both were "correct" in their own codebase.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: With Flutter, that sharing does not exist. You will reimplement the domain layer in Dart, and it will drift.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Conversely, if your web app is Angular, Vue, or server-rendered, there is nothing to share and this input is neutral — which frees Flutter to win on its own merits.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## Decision input 3: the CI reality

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: This is the part teams consistently underestimate, and it is where "one codebase" stops being true.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: One codebase does not mean one build. You still need:

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
- Two toolchains (Xcode and Android SDK), version-pinned and reproducible.
- macOS runners for iOS. These cost roughly 4-10× Linux runners.
- Two signing-credential paths: certificates and provisioning profiles for
  Apple, keystore for Android.
- Two store-submission pipelines with different review latencies and metadata.
- Device testing across OS versions on both platforms.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
```yaml
# The irreducible shape. "One codebase" does not collapse this.
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest        # cheap: unit tests, lint, typecheck

  build-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest        # cheap
    needs: test

  build-ios:
    runs-on: macos-14             # expensive, slower, flakier
    needs: test
```

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Two specifics worth knowing before you commit:

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: **Toolchain pinning is not optional.** An unpinned Xcode or Android Gradle Plugin version will break your build on a runner image update, on a day you did not plan to debug build infrastructure. Pin both, in the repo, and upgrade deliberately.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: **iOS signing is the most common CI failure for both frameworks.** Certificates expire, provisioning profiles need regenerating when you add a device or a capability, and the failure message is unhelpful. Use the platform's official automation (`fastlane match` or App Store Connect API keys), store it properly, and write down the renewal procedure, because the person who set it up will be on leave when it expires.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Neither framework helps with any of this. The build complexity is a property of shipping to two app stores, and it is roughly the same either way.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## Decision input 4: who you can hire

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Unglamorous, decisive.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
- **React Native**: hires from the React pool, which is large. A competent React
  engineer is productive in React Native in weeks. Native bridge work needs a
  Kotlin/Swift specialist, hired or contracted.
- **Flutter**: hires from the Flutter/Dart pool, which is smaller but genuinely
  enthusiastic and often more experienced in mobile specifically. Harder to
  hire quickly; frequently better mobile engineers when you do.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: For a team of three building one app, hiring speed probably decides it. For a team of fifteen with existing React people, the overlap decides it.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## The procedure

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text:
```
1. Count native capabilities needing a custom bridge.
   >= 2  -> weight heavily toward whichever language your team
            can staff bridges in. Framework choice is now secondary.

2. Is there a substantial React web codebase?
   yes  -> React Native, for the shared core package.
   no   -> neutral; continue.

3. Is the UI a controlled brand experience or a platform-conventional app?
   brand-controlled     -> Flutter.
   platform-conventional -> React Native.

4. Can you hire for Dart in your market, at your timeline?
   no -> React Native.

5. Still tied? Pick React Native if the team is web-leaning,
   Flutter if the team is mobile-leaning. Both are fine.
   Stop researching and start building.
```

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Step 5 is sincere. I have watched teams spend six weeks on this decision. Six weeks of building in either framework would have produced more information than six weeks of comparison, because the real constraints only show up when you hit them.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: ## The thing that actually doubles your team

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: A closing observation that applies regardless of which you pick.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: The cost that surprises people is not writing the code twice. It is **testing, releasing, and supporting twice** — two store review cycles, two sets of OS version compatibility, two crash-report streams, two sets of device-specific bugs, two release trains that drift out of sync.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: A cross-platform framework addresses the writing. It does almost nothing for the rest, and the rest is where the sustained effort lives. Pixorama's note on [shipping one product on two platforms without doubling the team](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/shipping-mobile-on-two-platforms) is mostly about that operational half, which is the half worth planning.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: For a straight framework-versus-framework treatment with the trade-offs laid out properly, their [React Native vs Flutter](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/react-native-vs-flutter) comparison covers the ground this post deliberately skips, and their round-up of [mobile app development firms and what each is good for](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-mobile-app-development-companies-india) is organised by specialism rather than by ranking, which is the more useful cut if your deciding input is native-bridge capability.

title: One codebase, two platforms: the cross-platform decision is a build-system problem
text: Read both frameworks' own architecture documentation before deciding — Flutter's rendering-pipeline docs and React Native's New Architecture docs are honest about their own trade-offs in a way third-party comparisons usually are not.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: # What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Someone quotes you $120,000 to build an app. You budget $120,000, maybe $150,000 with a contingency, and the app ships roughly on budget.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Then year two costs you another $90,000 and nobody warned you, because the quote was for the build and the build is the part of a mobile app with the clearest scope and the smallest total cost.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: I have now watched three apps through to their second year. The numbers below are from those three — two consumer, one B2B field-service — and I am giving ranges rather than averages because the variance is the interesting part.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## What the build quote covers

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Design, implementation, QA, store submission. Usually a fixed scope with a change-request process. If the quote came from a competent firm it is probably approximately right for the scope described, and scope creep during the build is a well-understood risk that everybody plans for.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Fine. That is the number you have. Here is what is not in it.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 1. The backend, if you did not already have one

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: This is the single largest omission I have seen in app budgets, and it happens because the conversation starts with "we need an app" and the app is the visible part.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: If the app needs accounts, sync, push notifications, an admin interface or any server-side business logic, that is a separate system. In the three projects: the backend was **40% to 70% of total engineering effort.**

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: The B2B one was 70%, because the app was essentially a client for a scheduling and inventory system that had to integrate with an existing ERP. The app was eight weeks. The integration was nine months.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: If a quote for "a mobile app" does not have a line for backend work, establish immediately whether that is because it is excluded or because nobody has thought about it. Those are very different situations and both are common.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 2. Two app stores, forever

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Not a one-off. An ongoing operational commitment:

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text:
- **Apple requires an annual developer account** and periodically requires
  rebuilds against a newer SDK to accept updates. Miss a deadline and you cannot
  ship.
- **Each OS release** (annually, both platforms) breaks something. Not always
  much. Always something. Budget two to four weeks of engineering per year per
  platform just to stay shippable, having added no features.
- **Review rejections** cost calendar time at the worst moment. We had a
  rejection over a subscription-flow technicality that cost eleven days against
  a marketing launch date.
- **Store metadata, screenshots and descriptions** need maintaining across
  locales every time the UI changes meaningfully.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Across the three projects this "do nothing, stay alive" cost ran **$18,000 to $35,000 a year**, with the variance driven mostly by how many OS versions and devices they supported.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: That last point is worth dwelling on: supporting iOS 15 as well as iOS 18 roughly doubles your device test matrix. The decision to drop old OS versions is a cost decision disguised as a product decision, and it is usually made by nobody.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 3. Crash and support load scales with installs, not features

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Once real users have it, you get a stream of reports that are device-specific, OS-version-specific, network-condition-specific, and frequently not reproducible on your desk.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: In the consumer apps, **post-launch bug work settled at roughly 25-30% of ongoing engineering capacity**, indefinitely. Not during a stabilisation period — as a steady state.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: This surprised everyone on all three projects. The mental model is that bugs are a launch phenomenon that decays. In mobile it does not decay, because the environment keeps changing underneath you: new devices, new OS versions, new network behaviours, users on three-year-old hardware.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Mobile has a characteristic that web does not: **you cannot fix forward immediately.** A bad release on the web is reverted in minutes. A bad mobile release sits in review for a day or more while your users have it, and a portion of your users will never update. One of the consumer apps still had 4% of its active base on a version eighteen months old.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: That changes the economics of testing. Mobile QA is worth more than web QA because the cost of a bad release is structurally higher.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 4. Analytics, crash reporting, and the rest of the stack

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Individually small, collectively not: crash reporting, analytics, push notification infrastructure, feature flags, over-the-air update capability, error tracking, session replay.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: **$500 to $4,000 a month** across the three, scaling with volume. The B2B app was at the low end; the consumer app with a large free tier was at the high end because analytics pricing is per-event and a chatty app generates a lot of events.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Worth checking: several of these price per monthly active user or per event, which means your infrastructure cost grows with the success metric you are trying to grow. Model it at 10× current users before you commit.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 5. The feature treadmill nobody budgets as a line

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: An app that does not change looks abandoned. Users notice, reviews mention it, and store ranking algorithms appear to favour recency.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: So you ship updates. Not necessarily big ones, but regularly. Across the three projects, **ongoing feature work ran 30-50% of the original build cost, per year.** The B2B app was lower, because its users had no alternative and did not care about freshness. The consumer apps were at the top of the range.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: This is the number that makes the total-cost picture land: a $120,000 build is plausibly a $60,000-a-year commitment thereafter, which over three years makes the build about 40% of the total.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## 6. The cross-platform decision, which cuts both ways

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Both consumer apps were cross-platform; the B2B one was native on both.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: What I observed: the cross-platform choice saved perhaps 30-40% on initial implementation and saved considerably less than that on the ongoing cost, because the ongoing cost is dominated by testing, releasing and supporting two platforms, which does not collapse.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: It also introduced a cost nobody forecast: **framework version upgrades.** A major version bump of a cross-platform framework is a project — dependency churn, breaking changes in community packages, native build configuration. We hit one of these that consumed six weeks.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Native avoids that and pays for it by writing everything twice. Across three years and three apps, my rough sense is that the total costs converge more than the initial quotes suggest, and the decision should therefore be made on team skills and native-capability needs rather than on projected cost savings — which is also roughly the conclusion of Pixorama's [the cross-platform decision](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/react-native-vs-flutter) write-up.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## Putting it together

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: For a $120,000 build quote, the three-year picture looked roughly like:

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text:
| | Low | High |
|---|---|---|
| Build (quoted) | $120,000 | $120,000 |
| Backend, if not existing | $80,000 | $280,000 |
| Store/OS maintenance, 3yr | $54,000 | $105,000 |
| Bug and support work, 3yr | $70,000 | $150,000 |
| Tooling and infrastructure, 3yr | $18,000 | $144,000 |
| Feature work, 3yr | $108,000 | $180,000 |
| **Three-year total** | **$450,000** | **$979,000** |

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: The quoted build is **12-27% of the three-year cost.**

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: I want to be careful about how much weight those numbers carry: they are three projects, in specific markets, with specific scopes. The ratios are more transferable than the absolute figures, and the ratio I would stand behind is that the build is somewhere between a sixth and a third of what you will spend over three years.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: For region-specific build pricing with the components broken out — which is the input to the first row rather than the whole table — Pixorama's [USA and Australia prices compared line by line](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-usa-australia) is more granular than anything I would attempt from three data points.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: ## What to do with this

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: Two things, both of which are cheap and almost never done:

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
