text: **Ask the quoting firm for their year-two and year-three estimate.** A good firm has one, because they maintain apps they have built and know what it costs. A firm that has not thought about it is quoting a build, not a product, and you should hold their number accordingly.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: **Decide the OS support policy before you start.** "We support the current and previous major OS version" is a single sentence that removes a recurring argument and a meaningful slice of the test matrix. Deciding it later means deciding it under pressure from a specific complaining customer.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: One last note on geography, since it changes the first row of that table more than anything else: the same scope quoted in different markets varies by a factor I would not have believed before seeing it. Their breakdown of [what a build costs in India, line by line](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-india) is a useful comparison point against the US and Australian figures, and the thing worth noticing is that the *ratio* of build to three-year total is roughly constant across markets. A cheaper build does not buy you a cheaper product; it buys you a cheaper sixth of one.

title: What a mobile app actually costs, after the quote
text: The app is not the project. The app is the part of the project you can see.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: # Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: The cross-platform promise is one codebase instead of two. It is true, and it is a smaller win than it sounds, because writing the code was never the expensive part.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: I have been close to three apps through to their second year — two cross-platform, one native on both. The cross-platform choice saved perhaps 30-40% on initial implementation. It saved considerably less than that on the ongoing cost, and the ongoing cost dominates.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: Here is where the money actually goes.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: ## What does not collapse

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: One codebase does not mean one of any of the following:

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two toolchains.** Xcode and the Android SDK, version-pinned and reproducible. An unpinned Xcode or Android Gradle Plugin version will break your build on a runner image update, on a day you had not planned to debug build infrastructure.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two release trains with different latencies.** Apple review is a day or more and occasionally much longer. Google is usually faster. So your "simultaneous release" is two releases that drift, and any coordinated feature launch is paced by the slower one.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two sets of OS releases to survive.** Annually, both platforms, and each one breaks something. Not always much, always something. Budget two to four weeks of engineering per year per platform purely to stay shippable, having added no features.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two signing-credential paths.** Certificates and provisioning profiles for Apple, a keystore for Android. iOS signing is the single most common CI failure I have seen on mobile projects, in both frameworks equally, and the failure message is unhelpful. Write down the renewal procedure, because the person who set it up will be on leave when it expires.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two device test matrices.** And this one is worse than it looks: supporting iOS 15 as well as iOS 18 roughly doubles your matrix. The decision to drop old OS versions is a cost decision disguised as a product decision, and in my experience it is made by nobody — it just drifts, and the matrix grows.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Two crash streams.** Device-specific, OS-version-specific, network-condition-specific, frequently not reproducible on your desk.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: None of that is affected by your framework choice. It is a property of shipping to two app stores.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: ## The number that reframes it

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: On the two consumer apps, post-launch bug work settled at roughly **25-30% of ongoing engineering capacity, indefinitely.** Not a stabilisation period — a steady state.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: This surprised everyone involved, including me. The mental model is that bugs are a launch phenomenon that decays. In mobile it does not decay, because the environment keeps changing underneath you: new devices, new OS versions, new network behaviours, and a long tail of users on three-year-old hardware.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: And mobile has a property that web does not: **you cannot fix forward immediately.** A bad web release is reverted in minutes. A bad mobile release sits in review while your users have it, and some portion of your users will never update — one of those apps still had 4% of its active base on a version eighteen months old.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: That single fact changes the economics of quality. Mobile QA is worth more than web QA, because the cost of a bad release is structurally higher and the remediation is slower. Teams that carry over web release instincts to mobile learn this expensively.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: ## So what actually keeps the team small

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: Four things, in order of how much they mattered:

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **1. Decide the OS support policy, in writing, before you start.** "We support the current and previous major version" is one sentence that removes a recurring argument and a meaningful slice of the test matrix. Deciding it later means deciding it under pressure from one complaining customer, which is how you end up supporting iOS 15 in 2026.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **2. Share the layer below the UI, not the UI.** On the React Native app this was the biggest real win and it was not what we expected. Sharing components with web mostly did not work. Sharing the layer underneath — API client, validation schemas, domain types, pricing rules — worked extremely well, and was about 35% of the code.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: The payoff was correctness more than effort. We had previously shipped a bug where web and mobile disagreed about whether a discount applied to shipping, and it took three weeks to find because both were correct in their own codebase. A rule that exists once cannot diverge.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **3. Automate the release, including the metadata.** Screenshots, descriptions and localised store copy are a surprising amount of manual work every time the UI changes meaningfully. Generating screenshots from UI tests is a day of setup and removes a recurring half-day.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **4. Instrument before you need it.** You cannot reproduce a user's crash on your desk. Breadcrumbs, session context and a correlation ID that survives into your backend logs are what turn "it crashes sometimes" into a fix.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: ## What I would not do

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Do not pick the framework on projected cost savings.** Across three years my rough sense is that total costs converge much more than the initial quotes suggest. Native writes everything twice; cross-platform pays a framework-upgrade tax — we hit one major version bump that consumed six weeks of dependency churn and native build configuration.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: Pick on team skills and native-capability needs instead. Specifically: count the platform capabilities you need that have no maintained package, because for each of those you are writing native code on both platforms regardless, and then the question is which language your team can staff bridges in.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: **Do not treat the app as the project.** If the app needs accounts, sync, push or server-side logic, that is a separate system, and on the three projects the backend was **40-70% of total engineering effort.** The B2B one was 70% — the app was eight weeks, the ERP integration was nine months.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: If a quote for "a mobile app" has no line for backend work, find out whether that is because it is excluded or because nobody has thought about it. Those are very different situations and both are common.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: ## The honest summary

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: A cross-platform framework addresses the writing. The writing is maybe a third of a mobile product's lifetime cost. Testing, releasing and supporting two platforms is most of the rest, and it is roughly the same either way.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: So the team does not double, but it does not halve either. What keeps it small is the OS support policy, sharing the domain layer, automating the release, and accepting that a quarter of your capacity is permanently allocated to the environment changing underneath you.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: My colleagues wrote about the operational half of this — [shipping one product on two platforms](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/shipping-mobile-on-two-platforms) — which is the half worth planning and the half that gets left out of estimates. And if you are at the quoting stage, [what the build itself costs in the US and Australia](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/mobile-app-development-cost-usa-australia) is more granular on the first line of the budget than I could be from three projects.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: The one question I would put to any firm quoting you a mobile build: *what is your year-two and year-three estimate?* A firm that maintains the apps it builds has an answer. A firm that does not is quoting a build, not a product, and you should weight their number accordingly.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: Next issue: security that does not stop delivery, and the one change I think most teams should make this quarter.

title: Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
Issue 8: Shipping on two platforms without doubling the team
text: *I am an engineer at [Pixorama](https://pixoramagroup.com/). Three apps, two consumer and one B2B field-service, anonymised. Percentages are from those three; treat the ratios as more transferable than the absolute figures.*

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: # Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: There are three ways to isolate tenant data, everyone picks the simplest one, and that is correct. The mistake is not the choice — it is implementing the simplest one in a way that makes moving to the others impossible, and then hitting the quarter where an enterprise prospect's security review requires it.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## The three models, honestly

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **Shared schema, tenant column.** One database, one set of tables, every row carries `tenant_id`. Cheapest to run, simplest to migrate, easiest to query across tenants for analytics. Isolation is enforced entirely by application correctness, which is the problem.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **Schema per tenant.** One database, one schema per tenant, identical tables. Isolation is structural. Costs you migration complexity (N schemas to migrate, transactionally, with partial-failure handling) and connection-pool pressure. Breaks down somewhere between 200 and 1,000 tenants depending on your migration tooling.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **Database per tenant.** Full isolation, per-tenant backup and restore, per-tenant encryption keys, straightforward data residency. Operationally heaviest by a wide margin, and the only model that satisfies the strictest procurement requirements.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **Pick shared schema.** For almost any new SaaS, at any plausible early scale, it is the right answer, and the people who tell you to start with database-per-tenant are describing an operational burden that will consume the runway you needed for product work.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: The rest of this post is about implementing it so that the day you need per-tenant databases for your three largest customers, you can do it.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## The failure that defines the problem

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: That second function returns every tenant's financial data to whoever calls it. It passes code review, because the reviewer is looking at a summary query and nothing about it looks dangerous. It passes tests, because the test database has one tenant.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: This is not a hypothetical class of bug. It is *the* multi-tenancy bug, it is reported in real products regularly, and the reason it keeps happening is that correctness depends on a developer remembering something, on every query, forever.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: So do not depend on that.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## Enforce isolation below the application

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: PostgreSQL row-level security moves the `WHERE` clause from the application into the database. The query above returns zero rows instead of everyone's.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text:
```sql
-- Every tenant-scoped table gets this treatment.
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to table owner too

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
```

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Two details that matter:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **`FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.** Without it, the table owner bypasses the policy. Your application frequently connects as the owner, which would make the whole thing decorative.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **`WITH CHECK` as well as `USING`.** `USING` filters reads; `WITH CHECK` constrains writes. Without the second one, a tenant can insert rows belonging to another tenant — a less obvious but equally real hole.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Then set the tenant once per request, in one place:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text:
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tenant_scope(conn, tenant_id):
    """set_config(..., true) makes it transaction-local, so it cannot
    leak to the next request that borrows this pooled connection.
    Getting this wrong is worse than having no RLS at all."""
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", (str(tenant_id),))
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        pass   # transaction end clears it
```

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: The `true` third argument is load-bearing. `set_config(..., false)` is session-scoped, and with a connection pool that means request N+1 inherits request N's tenant. That is a worse bug than the one you were preventing, because it is intermittent and load-dependent.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Wire it into the request lifecycle so no handler can skip it:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: `resolve_tenant` reads a signed token claim. Never a request header or a URL path segment the client controls — that converts your isolation boundary into a parameter the attacker supplies.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## The escape hatch, and how to make it loud

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: You will need cross-tenant queries: platform analytics, support tooling, billing reconciliation. The temptation is a connection that bypasses RLS, used "carefully".

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Make it a separate role, a separate pool, and audited:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: If a developer can reach cross-tenant data by picking a different connection from the same pool, they will, under deadline, and it will not be noticed in review. If it requires a decorator, a role, and a written reason that lands in an audit log, it gets used for the four legitimate cases and nothing else.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## Testing isolation, which is the part that gets skipped

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: One test, parameterised over every tenant-scoped table, that fails if a table is missing its policy:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text:
```python
TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES = discover_tables_with_column("tenant_id")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("table", TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES)
def test_rls_enabled(db, table):
    row = db.query_one("""
        SELECT relrowsecurity, relforcerowsecurity
        FROM pg_class WHERE relname = %s
    """, (table,))
    assert row.relrowsecurity, f"{table} has tenant_id but RLS is OFF"
    assert row.relforcerowsecurity, f"{table} does not FORCE RLS"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("table", TENANT_SCOPED_TABLES)
def test_cannot_read_other_tenant(db, table, two_tenants):
    a, b = two_tenants
    seed_row(table, tenant_id=b)
    with tenant_scope(db, a):
        rows = db.query(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
        assert all(r.tenant_id == a for r in rows)
```

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Discovering the table list from the schema rather than hardcoding it is the whole point: the test fails when someone adds a new table with a `tenant_id` and forgets the policy, which is exactly the moment you want to find out.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Also: **make your test and dev databases multi-tenant by default.** Seed two tenants, always. The single-tenant dev database is why the summary-query bug survives to production.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: ## Keeping the door open to per-tenant databases

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: The migration you will eventually be asked for: move tenant 7 to its own database, because they signed a contract that requires it.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Three things, done now, make that a week instead of a quarter:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **1. Resolve tenants to a connection, not to a constant.**

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text:
```python
# Even while every tenant is on the same database, route through
# a lookup. Today it returns the same DSN for everyone. The day it
# doesn't, nothing above this layer changes.
class TenantRouter:
    def dsn_for(self, tenant_id):
        placement = self.placements.get(tenant_id)
        return placement.dsn if placement else self.default_dsn
```

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: This is maybe thirty lines and it is the difference between a configuration change and a refactor of every call site.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **2. Keep `tenant_id` on every row even when it becomes redundant.** In a per-tenant database it is technically unnecessary. Keep it anyway: it makes the extraction a straightforward filtered copy, it keeps the schema identical across placements, and it means the RLS policies still work and still protect you if a tenant is ever consolidated back.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: **3. Never let a foreign key cross tenants.** Enforce it:

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text:
```sql
-- Composite FKs including tenant_id make cross-tenant references
-- structurally impossible, and make per-tenant extraction a clean cut.
ALTER TABLE invoice_lines
```

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret
text: Shared schema with `tenant_id`. RLS with `FORCE` and `WITH CHECK`. Transaction-local `set_config`. Tenant from a token claim, set in middleware. A deliberately awkward audited escape hatch. Schema-discovered isolation tests. Composite foreign keys including `tenant_id`. A tenant-to-connection router that does nothing yet.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation for an early SaaS, and the migration you will regret

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: # Why every "top 10 companies" list looks the same

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: Search for the best software development companies in any country and you will get dozens of near-identical pages. Ten to fifteen firms, a paragraph each, a "what to look for when choosing" section, an FAQ. Different sites, overlapping firms, same structure, same adjectives.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: I should disclose up front that I have a stake in this: I have been listed on these pages, I have paid to be listed on one, and I have written one. So treat what follows as an insider's account rather than a disinterested one.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: The sameness is not laziness. It is the predictable output of the economics, and understanding the economics tells you exactly which parts of these pages to trust.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## Four kinds of page, which look identical

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The directory.** Clutch, GoodFirms and similar. Their business is listings; firms claim profiles, collect verified client reviews, and pay for placement in sponsored positions. The reviews are often genuinely verified, which makes these the most useful of the four — but the *ordering* is a mix of review score, activity and spend.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The lead-gen site.** Exists to rank for "best X companies", collect enquiries, and sell them. Listed firms frequently pay per listing or per lead. The assessment is whatever the writer did in an afternoon. These are the majority of results for most queries.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The competitor's content marketing.** A firm writes "the best X companies" and lists itself first or second, with nine plausible competitors around it. The nine are chosen partly for credibility and partly for not being a direct threat in the author's own market.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The occasional real review.** A journalist or analyst with a methodology. Rare, and usually behind a paywall or published by an analyst firm.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: From the outside, all four render as a page with ten names on it, and nothing in the page's design tells you which you are reading.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## Why the content converges

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: Four forces, each individually reasonable:

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The query is the brief.** Someone searching "best mobile app development companies" wants a list. The page that ranks is the page that most directly provides a list. Every publisher is optimising against the same query, so every page converges on the same shape. There is no competitive advantage in being structurally different, and a real penalty for it.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The research cost is high and the differentiation value is low.** Genuinely assessing fifteen development firms means reading code, talking to their clients, understanding their delivery process — weeks of expert time. It is not recoverable from the page's revenue, and no reader can tell from the page whether you did it. So nobody does.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **The source material is the firms' own marketing.** Every entry is written from the company's website and case studies. They all describe themselves as having senior engineers, transparent communication and a client-first approach. Summarise fifteen of those and you get fifteen indistinguishable paragraphs, because the input was fifteen indistinguishable positioning statements.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **Everyone reads each other's lists.** When compiling one, the fastest way to assemble candidates is to read existing lists. This produces convergence on the same names, which then appear on more lists, which makes them appear more credible. A firm's presence on these lists is substantially a function of having previously been on these lists.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: That last mechanism is the one worth internalising, because it means **list frequency measures marketing persistence, not quality.** The firms that appear everywhere are the firms that have been doing content and outreach for five years. That is genuinely informative — it means they are established and reasonably professional — but it is not what the page claims to be telling you.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## What these pages are actually good for

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: Not nothing. Two things:

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **Candidate discovery.** You will find names you had not heard of. That is real value, and it is the only value. Read six lists, collect every name, and you have a reasonable longlist of firms that exist and are active in your market.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **Negative signal.** A firm that appears on *no* list in a market where lists are plentiful is either very new, very small, or not doing any outbound marketing. Any of those might be fine — some of the best boutiques do no marketing at all — but it is worth asking why.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: What they are not good for: **ordering, assessment, or fit.** Position one is not better than position seven. The adjectives are from the firm's own website. And the question you actually have — can this specific firm do this specific thing for my specific constraints — is not addressable by a page that has never met you.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## How to read one properly

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: Five checks that take about ten minutes:

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **1. Find the money.** Look for "sponsored", "partner", "advertiser disclosure", affiliate parameters in the outbound links, or a "get listed" page in the navigation. A "get listed" link means the list is a product. That does not make it worthless — it makes the ordering commercial.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **2. Check who published it.** If it is a firm in the same industry, the list is content marketing and the ordering reflects the author's interests. This includes lists where the author does not appear: they may be positioning adjacent to the names, or the page may exist to rank and capture enquiries.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **3. Look for a methodology, and then look for evidence of it.** Many pages claim one. Few show their work. "We evaluated on experience, portfolio and client feedback" with no indication of what was found is a sentence, not a method. What would convince me: a named data source, a count of reviews examined, a stated exclusion.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **4. Check the dates.** Pages titled "2026" are frequently 2022 pages with the year edited. Look at whether any entry references anything recent. A list that has not been genuinely revisited is describing a market that has moved.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: **5. Ignore the order entirely and use the names.** This is the main practical advice. Treat the page as an unordered set of candidates, then do your own assessment.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## The honest disclosure

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: I said I would be specific about my own interest, so: the firm I am associated with publishes pages of exactly this kind. There is a set of them on [Pixorama's blog](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog), including [their Australian SEO roundup](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia), and everything in this post applies to those too.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: They are written from public information, including the firms' own marketing. They have not involved talking to those firms' clients. They exist in part because people search for this and it is a reasonable way to be found. If you read one, use it for the names and apply the five checks, same as any other.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: I do not think that is cynical. The pages are genuinely useful for candidate discovery and I would rather say what they are than pretend to a methodology nobody applies. The failure in this genre is not that the pages exist; it is that they are written in the register of an assessment when they are a directory.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: ## What would actually be useful

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: If anyone wants to build a better version, the gap is clear and it is not a content gap.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: The useful artefact is not a ranked list. It is a **comparison on dimensions a buyer can act on**: team size, actual location of the delivery team (not the sales office), named technologies with depth evidence, typical engagement size, minimum contract, whether they will work inside your codebase or only on projects, and who you would be reporting to.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: None of that is in any list I have read, including the ones I have written, because the firms do not publish it and collecting it means asking fifteen companies fifteen questions and getting answers from maybe six.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: Which is the actual reason every one of these pages looks the same: the information that would differentiate them is information nobody has, and the information everybody has is the firms' own marketing copy.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: I will give one example of a page doing better than the genre requires, partly because it is my employer's and I should be consistent about disclosing that. Their [comparison of software development companies in India](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-software-development-companies-india) states in the body that Pixorama is one of the ten listed. That one sentence is rarer than it should be, and it is the minimum I would want from any page in this format — not because disclosure makes the ordering neutral, but because it tells you which of the four kinds of page you are reading, which is the thing the genre otherwise hides.

title: Why every 'top 10 companies' list looks the same
text: So read six, take the names, and go and ask the questions yourself. That part has never been outsourceable.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: # Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Last issue. Thank you for reading, and particularly to the people who replied with disagreements — three of those changed what I wrote in issues four and seven.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: I have saved the thing I get asked about most, and about which I have the least systematic view. How do you choose a vendor — an agency, a development firm, a platform — when every one of them is good at being chosen?

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Three parts: why the published comparisons do not help, why the pitch selects for the wrong qualities, and the six questions that do most of the work.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## Part one: the lists are directories, written in the register of assessments

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Search for the best anything-companies in any market and you will get dozens of near-identical pages. Ten to fifteen firms, a paragraph each, a "what to look for" section, an FAQ.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: I should disclose that my own employer publishes pages of exactly this kind, [including ones my own colleagues publish](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/best-seo-agencies-australia) for the Australian market. Everything below applies to those too.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: They are written from public information — mostly the firms' own marketing material. They have not involved talking to those firms' clients. They exist in part because people search for this, and that is a reasonable way to be found.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The reason they all look the same is economic rather than lazy:

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **Genuinely assessing fifteen firms** means reading their code, talking to their clients, understanding their delivery process. Weeks of expert time, not recoverable from the page, and no reader can tell from the page whether you did it. So nobody does.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **The source material is identical.** Every firm describes itself as having senior engineers, transparent communication and a client-first approach. Summarise fifteen of those and you get fifteen indistinguishable paragraphs, because the input was fifteen indistinguishable positioning statements.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **Everyone reads each other's lists.** The fastest way to assemble candidates is to read existing lists, which produces convergence on the same names, which makes those names look more credible, which gets them onto more lists.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: That last mechanism is the important one: **list frequency measures marketing persistence, not quality.** Firms that appear everywhere have been doing content and outreach for five years. That is genuinely informative — they are established and reasonably professional — but it is not what the page claims to measure.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: So: use these pages for **candidate discovery only.** Read six, collect every name, ignore the ordering entirely. That is real value and it is the only value.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## Part two: the pitch selects for confidence

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The standard pitch is: an audit with a number of problems found, a gap analysis showing you behind competitors, case studies with percentage improvements, and a proposal with a retainer and deliverables.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Every element establishes that there is a problem and that they have a process. None establishes that their process caused the results in their case studies, which is the only thing you are buying.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: And the format has converged because it works on buyers. Which means the selection process rewards the firms best at pitching, and pitching skill is roughly uncorrelated with delivery skill.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Good work in most of these fields is unglamorous. It consists of doing sensible things patiently, and the people who do it tend to present *less* impressively, because their story has fewer numbers and more caveats. The structural problem is that the pitch rewards confidence and the work rewards patience.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## Part three: the six questions

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: These are the ones that produce genuinely different answers from good and bad vendors. I have used them on agencies, development firms and platform vendors, and they transfer.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **1. "What were the absolute numbers, before and after?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Case studies are quoted in percentages because percentages are chosen to be large. 340% growth from 200 to 880 is real on a tiny baseline and tells you nothing about a mature system.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Ask for absolute figures, the time period, and the starting position. Then ask the follow-up that separates asset-builders from rank-renters: *what happened in the twelve months after the engagement ended?*

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **2. "Which of those results would have happened anyway?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: This produces the most interesting silence of the six.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Outcomes improve for lots of reasons: the market grew, a competitor exited, there was a PR event, a product launched, paid spend increased. A good vendor has thought hard about attribution, because they want credit for the right things — they will segment, reference a baseline, and separate branded from non-branded effects unprompted.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: A vendor who has never considered the counterfactual is either not analytical or relying on you not to ask.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **3. "What will you do in month one that is not an audit?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Audits are the vendor's cheapest deliverable and your least valuable one. A tool produces one in twenty minutes.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: This question tests whether they have a thesis about *your* situation. A good answer sounds like a hypothesis with a mechanism: "your category pages compete with your blog for the same terms and the blog wins, which is why the commercial pages don't convert — we'd fix that first." A bad answer is a list of deliverables.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **4. "What is the binding constraint, and is it something you can fix?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The question underneath every engagement. Frequently the real constraint is something the vendor cannot touch: a six-week engineering queue, a product that does not convert, a market dominated by three incumbents you will not outrank.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: A good vendor names it, including when naming it costs them the sale. I have had one tell me "you have a six-week dev queue; recommendations you cannot implement are not worth paying for, fix that first" — and that firm got the work eighteen months later because I remembered.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **5. "What would make you tell me to stop paying you?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The same question from the other side, and it tests whether they have located the boundary of their own usefulness. A vendor with no answer will keep invoicing past it, not from malice but because nobody has defined where "done" is.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: **6. "Who specifically does the work, how many other accounts do they carry, and can I speak to them before signing?"**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The person pitching is often not the person delivering. Fine if disclosed.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Then do the arithmetic out loud: divide the retainer by a plausible blended rate and see how many hours you are buying. Twelve accounts per person means roughly three hours a month on yours. The gap between that number and the promised deliverables is the honest measure of the proposal.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## The thing underneath all six

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Each asks the same question in a different register: **is there a causal story, and can you show me the mechanism?**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: That is the only reliable signal I have found, and it is reliable because it is hard to fake under follow-up questions. Confidence is easy to perform. A causal story that survives three "why" questions is not.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## What I would actually build instead

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: If anyone wants to make something better than the comparison lists, the gap is clear, and it is not a content gap.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: The useful artefact is not a ranking. It is a comparison on dimensions a buyer can act on: team size, the actual location of the delivery team rather than the sales office, named technologies with evidence of depth, typical engagement size, minimum contract, whether they will work inside your codebase or only on discrete projects, and who you would report to.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: None of that is in any list I have read, including the ones my colleagues write, because the firms do not publish it and collecting it means asking fifteen companies fifteen questions and getting answers from perhaps six.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Which is the real reason these pages all look the same: the information that would differentiate them is information nobody has, and the information everybody has is marketing copy.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: And frequently the answer to the whole exercise is that you do not need a vendor at all — you need two engineering sprints and someone with the authority to decide what the system is for. That build-versus-buy-versus-hire question is one my colleagues wrote up as [in-house versus outsourced](https://pixoramagroup.com/blog/how-to-choose-software-development-company), and it is worth settling before you start reading comparison pages, because the pages assume the answer.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: ## Closing the series

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Ten issues on one claim: **almost every expensive technology surprise is a structural decision showing up late.**

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Migration costs that were a wave-ordering decision. Cloud bills that were a service-boundary decision. Rewrites that were a working-conditions problem mislabelled as an architecture problem. Agent projects that were workflow projects. RAG systems that were content projects. Augmentation failures that were contract failures. Mobile costs that were an OS-support-policy decision. Security programmes that were a control-selection decision.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: In every case the information was available at the time, and in every case nobody was looking, because the question had been assigned to a different function.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: I do not have a clean solution to that, and I distrust anyone who claims one. The best I have is the habit: when something costs more than expected, do not ask what went wrong. Ask **which decision, made earlier, in a different department, is now arriving.** The answer is usually findable, and it is usually not where the post-mortem is looking.

title: Issue 10: How to run a vendor shortlist
text: Thank you for reading. If I start a second series it will be about the gap between what an architecture diagram asserts and what the system does, which is a subject I have been avoiding because I do not yet know what I think.
